gaps: The 1953 and 1954 Cottet papers and the 1962 Thorp–Waring Nature paper were located but not read; their titles or metadata are not evidence of causal history or accidental exposure.

Thorp's 1963 original was read only as an abstract reproduced by a third-party reference listing; its full discussion of selection rationale was not read. The explicit French-work-to-selection causal link rests on the later historical accounts.

Boucherle's French full text was not read. The accessible abstract supports a bounded chemical connection to fenofibrate but not a complete account of inventorship, priority, or comparative clinical performance.

classes.name: Iron replacement preparations

starting.description: Clinical reports described pallor improving with iron in chlorosis. Blaud explicitly started from existing iron treatment and its inconsistent outcomes, then proposed a modified preparation and regimen; the first reason anyone tried iron remains unknown.

inspiration.description: Reported clinical improvement from iron-containing remedies for chlorosis, with Blaud explicitly developing a different regimen from already-known but variably effective iron treatment; the first motivating experiment is not identified.

steps.description: A historical account attributes improvement in pallor following an iron treatment course to Sydenham; iron was used for chlorosis before deficiency was established as its cause.
Blaud described variable outcomes with existing iron remedies and proposed a sulfate-plus-potassium-subcarbonate pill and higher-dose regimen; he stated that iron carbonate formed in the mixture.
Smart compared iron preparations already in use and recorded a patient whose haemoglobin rose during sulfate-of-iron treatment.
By 1960 sulfate was established and fumarate was among later oral preparations advertised as alternatives; Hayhoe questioned a general comparative advantage.

design.description: Blaud deliberately modified an existing iron remedy by combining iron sulfate and potassium subcarbonate in pills and increasing the regimen; he asserted that iron carbonate formed and proposed improved absorption or activity. Later oral salts including fumarate were offered as alternatives to sulfate with claims of improved performance. The final pill composition was not independently tested here, and the originator's rationale for fumarate is not established.

circumstances.description: Blaud deliberately proposed a changed iron preparation and dosing regimen to address perceived failures of existing treatment; whether the first therapeutic discovery of iron was planned is unknown.

classes.name: 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors

starting.description: The program developed from a biological relationship between testosterone, DHT, the 5-alpha-reductase enzyme, and androgen-dependent tissues, with human inherited enzyme deficiency later accelerating the work. The investigators' subsequent clinical rationale included the small prostates observed in adults with inherited deficiency.

inspiration.description: Endocrine conversion of testosterone to DHT and clinical studies of inherited 5-alpha-reductase deficiency supplied the biological rationale. The 1986 chemistry article summarizes an additional clinical prostate observation from an earlier report.

steps.description: A Merck BPH project drew on androgen biology and recognition of the testosterone-to-DHT conversion.
Human enzyme-deficiency reports accelerated the work and were followed by a decision to screen for inhibitors.

Earlier steroid screening found enzyme inhibition in vitro but not in intact animals; a search for less readily reduced inhibitors produced active 4-azasteroids, followed by structure–activity investigation.

Rasmusson and Reynolds synthesized the inhibitor MK-906, which was selected for development and later marketed as finasteride. The exact date of its synthesis relative to the 1986 report is not established here.

A 1986 paper documented additional structure–activity studies using human and rat prostatic enzyme and rat androgen-receptor assays to identify potent, selective inhibitors; its publication date does not establish when MK-906 was synthesized.

design.description: Researchers deliberately screened steroid compounds, sought agents less susceptible to reductive metabolism, synthesized azasteroid derivatives, varied A-ring and C-17 structures while measuring enzyme and receptor activity, and synthesized MK-906; the underlying biological relationship preceded this design work.

circumstances.description: Merck's screening for a 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor was planned; the original clinical observations are a separate stage.

classes.name: Folate replacement preparations

starting.description: Wills investigated tropical macrocytic anaemia using the observed benefit of liver in another anaemia and animal evidence of a vitamin B-complex deficiency; her patients improved with liver or yeast preparations. In parallel, investigators observed that animal nutrition and bacterial growth depended on factors in natural extracts, and used those biological responses to investigate and isolate related factors. The record does not establish that every microbial research group was directly motivated by Wills.

inspiration.description: Observed clinical responses to yeast and liver preparations, animal dietary-deficiency and treatment responses, and the growth requirements of microorganisms supplied biological leads. The starting materials included yeast, liver and green plant extracts; the clinical and microbiological routes were not a single proven chain of individual motivations.

steps.description: A recognized liver-treatment effect and Wills's animal observations prompted tests of liver and yeast extract in tropical macrocytic anaemia; she reported patient improvements while leaving the responsible factor unidentified.

Independent investigations of chick nutritional deficiency and microbial growth factors in extracts helped drive isolation and identification of related folate-active factors. Wilkinson reports that synthetic pteroylglutamic acid matched a crystalline liver L. casei factor.

Chemists developed synthesis routes to a defined pteroylglutamic acid preparation and compared the product with the liver factor by physical measurements and bioassay; a 1948 original report explicitly follows previous synthesis work.

Clinicians used the synthetic preparation orally in an early nutritional macrocytic anaemia case series and reported haematological improvement, subject to the study's diagnostic and treatment limitations.

design.description: Researchers used growth and nutritional assays to isolate and characterize factors, developed chemical routes to a defined oxidized pteroylglutamic acid product, checked its properties against the liver factor, and administered synthetic material orally in capsules. These deliberate developments followed observed biological activity; the later 1948 synthetic route did not establish a from-scratch founding activity concept.

circumstances.description: Wills's selection and test of yeast extract followed her animal-deficiency hypothesis; the 1948 chemists deliberately developed a further route to a known factor. This labels those stages, not every discovery in the class.

The review distinguishes oxidized folic acid from the broader family of natural reduced and conjugated folates, and presents the isolation-artifact explanation as a qualified hypothesis.
The 1946 treatment series was small and uncontrolled, with diagnostic uncertainty and concurrent or subsequent care; it establishes early use and reported responses, not a modern efficacy estimate.
This bounded founding history does not establish the origin or efficacy of every later indication, formulation or other folate compound.
conflicts: Wilkinson cites 1945 and 1946 syntheses, while Zheng and Cantley describe structural-elucidation work culminating in 1948. Hultquist's 1948 report itself refers to previous synthesis. classes.name: Gabapentinoids

starting.description: The founding programs drew on the endogenous inhibitory neurotransmitter GABA and its relationship to seizures. For gabapentin, the reported concept was to modify GABA to improve central nervous system penetration while retaining GABA-like pharmacology. In the separate pregabalin program, GABA physiology and prior anticonvulsant effects of GABA-degrading-enzyme inhibitors motivated selective, more lipophilic analogues; unexpected activation of the GABA-producing enzyme by an already synthesized series then prompted anticonvulsant testing.

inspiration.description: Endogenous GABA and the observed relationship between inhibitory GABA biology and seizures motivated both programs. In Silverman's branch, prior anticonvulsant effects of enzyme inhibitors and the subsequent unexpected in-vitro effect of synthesized analogues led to testing; neither the natural origin nor the therapeutic GABA mechanism of the final drugs is claimed.

steps.description: GABA was known as an inhibitory neurotransmitter, and Silverman's retrospective describes brain GABA administration stopping seizures and previous anticonvulsant effects of GABA-AT inhibitors. The historical review attributes the gabapentin concept to improving GABA's CNS penetration while retaining its pharmacology.

Gabapentin's inventors prepared cyclic amino acids, including the structure in patent Example 1. They reported unexpected animal protection against chemically induced convulsions for the series; the cited patent passage does not assign a quantitative outcome to gabapentin specifically.

In the separate pregabalin research program, Silverman and colleagues designed more lipophilic GABA and glutamate analogues in search of selective GABA-AT inhibition. After synthesis, the GABA-analogue series unexpectedly activated GAD in vitro, and Silverman sought anticonvulsant testing.

Testing found 3-isobutyl-GABA particularly active against mouse seizures. According to the discoverer, the active S isomer became pregabalin and was prepared at larger scale. The 1992 abstract explicitly left the proposed GAD mechanism unestablished in vivo.

The 1993 study linked anticonvulsant stereoselectivity of 3-isobutyl-GABA to displacement at a gabapentin-labeled binding site. In 1996 the gabapentin-binding protein was identified as a calcium-channel α2δ subunit; a later review groups both medicines as α2δ ligands. This target was identified after, not assumed as the historical starting point of, the GABA-inspired programs.

design.description: Researchers designed cyclic or 3-substituted synthetic GABA analogues to improve brain access and/or selectively alter GABA-related enzymes, screened biological activity, and developed synthesis of the active S enantiomer of 3-isobutyl-GABA. These were substantive chemical and pharmacological innovations rather than mere extraction of natural GABA; the subsequent α2δ binding was not the original proposed GABA mechanism.

circumstances.description: The GABA-analogue design and enzyme testing were planned; Silverman describes the post-synthesis GAD activation as unexpected, and the inventors' patent describes the broader cyclic series' animal anticonvulsant protection as surprising. These statements concern particular stages, not chance versus intent for every development step.

classes.name: Sulfonylureas

starting.description: Unexpected hypoglycaemia during treatment with a synthetic antibacterial sulfonamide supplied the clinical starting observation. Investigators then tested pancreatic dependence, inferred insulin secretion and developed the therapeutic class.

inspiration.description: A clinical effect of synthetic2254RP followed by pancreatic/insulin physiology. No naturally isolated molecular scaffold is needed for the approved observation-led interpretation.

steps.description: Clinical hypoglycaemic events during antibacterial2254RP treatment prompted investigation.
Physiological experiments showed pancreatic dependence and supported an insulin-secretory interpretation and therapeutic proposal.
Later carbutamide/tolbutamide observations and clinical development established the oral hypoglycaemic class; individual later analogues are outside scope.

design.description: The programme deliberately investigated mechanism and related structures after the clinical signal, then developed and evaluated therapeutic sulfonylureas. The initiating adverse effect was not an activity first designed from scratch.

circumstances.description: The clinical hypoglycaemia was unexpected; subsequent animal/physiological and therapeutic studies were deliberate.

classes.name: Organic nitrate vasodilators

starting.description: Brunton witnessed experimental vascular effects of amyl nitrite and reported angina relief; Murrell connected nitroglycerin's physiological effects to that comparator and predicted benefit. Separately, prior sugar-alcohol nitrate depressor effects prompted the Krantz laboratory to study sugar-anhydride nitrates, including an isosorbide nitrate.

inspiration.description: Experimental vascular and clinical effects of amyl nitrite, physiological effects of nitroglycerin, and known depressor effects of sugar-alcohol nitrate compounds supplied starting observations in different episodes. Amyl nitrite is a nitrite comparator, not a nitrate class member.

steps.description: Brunton combined observed amyl-nitrite effects on arterial tension with an angina case and reported pain relief after a deliberate therapeutic test.
Murrell connected nitroglycerin's physiological effects with amyl nitrite and anticipated benefit in angina, then compared their pulse tracings.
Murrell described relief of anginal episodes after administering dilute nitroglycerin.
The 1939 anhydride-nitrate series included table-named isosorbide dinitrate tested for blood-pressure effects in dogs (E6).
Carr's retrospective dates a report to 1940, but the named compound was already reported in 1939; Silber separately dates synthesis to 1938. Exact synthesis priority remains unresolved.

A separate historical abstract describes Porjé's Swedish research on isosorbide dinitrate and marketing in Sweden in 1946, without establishing the initiating idea or its connection to the U.S. studies.
A mononitrate was reported as an in-vivo dinitrate metabolite in 1967; isosorbide-5-mononitrate was described as an active metabolite in clinical use by 1990.

design.description: Murrell deliberately compared physiological responses and clinically tested a dilute solution of an already available compound. The Krantz laboratory then prepared a different series of sugar-anhydride nitrate structures for pharmacological investigation, rather than merely changing delivery.

circumstances.description: Murrell's angina trial followed a stated physiological analogy; the 1939 laboratory's synthesis and pharmacological study of anhydride nitrates followed prior depressor observations. This describes these deliberate research stages, not every finding or a blanket absence of chance.

classes.name: Hydrazinophthalazine direct arteriolar vasodilators

starting.description: According to Sneader, a blood-pressure fall and peripheral dilation were observed during Ciba's synthetic imidazoline investigations; the laboratory expanded to other nitrogen heterocycles and hypotensive screening of phthalazines yielded hydralazine, though why it expanded is not expressly stated. Chast instead directly reports diversion after a hypotensive effect appeared in an antimalarial search. Both are retrospective accounts; the primary evidence read here does not resolve the initial program.

inspiration.description: Chast directly attributes the change to a hypertension application to hydralazine's observed effect during an antimalarial search. Sneader describes an earlier blood-pressure/peripheral-vascular effect of synthetic imidazolines, followed by expanded screening that yielded hydralazine, but does not expressly identify the reason for expansion. This classification uses Ha's broad biological-inspiration definition and does not imply a natural-source scaffold.

steps.description: A historical review describes blood-pressure lowering in an imidazoline series, followed by exploration of other nitrogen heterocycles and hypotensive screening of phthalazines.

Chast's historical account directly links hydralazine's observed circulatory effect during an antimalarial search to its application for hypertension; the upstream purpose differs from Sneader's account.

In their 1949 patent the inventors described a preparation of 1-hydrazinophthalazine and claimed pressure-lowering effects for their compounds; the 1950 original report described the pharmacological properties of substituted phthalazines.
The 1951 chemistry abstract describes modification of the ring system and hydrazine group in related compounds, without establishing a particular optimization sequence.

A 1952 clinical study measured cardiovascular and renal effects of the named compound and interpreted its hemodynamic action as peripheral vascular relaxation, while the site of action remained uncertain.

design.description: Ciba researchers screened related phthalazine structures and identified hydralazine as a long-acting peripheral dilator according to a later history; the inventors' patent describes chemical synthesis. The 1951 chemistry abstract describes ring and hydrazine-group substitutions. A specific causal optimization sequence or superiority of individual alterations is not established by the material read.

circumstances.description: The historical review describes screening the phthalazine series for hypotensive activity; this does not settle whether the original effect or the initial synthesis was unexpected.

classes.name: ACE inhibitors

starting.description: Renin–angiotensin physiology and observed venom-peptide ACE inhibition supplied the biological starting point. Teprotide then demonstrated a working therapeutic effect; subsequent biochemical observations and a hypothetical active-site model enabled oral small-molecule development.

inspiration.description: Venom-peptide activity, renin–angiotensin/enzyme physiology and observed inhibitor chemistry informed a hypothetical binding model. The theoretical design is a later contribution within an observation-led lineage.

steps.description: Physiological/clinical questions about the renin–angiotensin system prompted a deliberate search for ACE inhibitors.
Venom peptides supplied potent working inhibition. Teprotide showed blood-pressure lowering in patients, but poor oral activity limited drug development.
Biochemical homology with carboxypeptidase A, peptide structure-activity work and a known product-analogue inhibitor informed the hypothetical ACE model and new small inhibitors.
Testing hypothesized interactions and zinc-binding substitutions produced captopril. Its smaller nonpeptide architecture supplied oral activity and helped establish the useful class.

design.description: The investigators constructed and tested a hypothetical binding model, designed a new small-molecule architecture and optimized functional groups and zinc binding. They also addressed oral exposure. These contributions are substantial and are retained explicitly without erasing the preceding observed biology and working inhibitors.

circumstances.description: The documented ACE-inhibitor project, peptide investigation and model-guided chemistry were deliberate. No accidental origin of the entire class is inferred.

classes.name: ENaC-blocking potassium-sparing diuretics

starting.description: For the triamterene branch, a reported kidney-growth response to a butterfly-wing pteridine pigment prompted investigation and testing of related pteridines; Gorecki identifies the pigment as xanthopterin. A separate pyrazine branch began with observed diuretic activity during screening of synthetic folate-antagonist intermediates.

inspiration.description: The triamterene pteridine program followed a biological response to a butterfly pigment, identified in the dissertation as xanthopterin, and was advanced by the observed diuretic effects of synthetic pteridines. The distinct pyrazine branch followed diuretic activity observed while screening synthetic intermediates.

steps.description: A reported pteridine-related kidney effect motivated a hypothesis about renal function and a directed screen of pteridines in rats.

Observed diuretic activity in SKF 371 prompted further testing. The diuretic SKF 6874 caused potassium loss, but its activity suggested further polyaminoarylpteridines; triamterene displayed sodium excretion with reduced potassium excretion in sodium-deficient rats.
The participant retrospective reports promising triamterene tests in 1958 and clinical trials by 1960.
In a separate pyrazine branch, a diuretic effect observed during screening of synthetic folate-antagonist intermediates led through chemical substitution to amiloride.

design.description: Researchers synthesized and tested pteridines, explored changes in amino and aryl substitution, and identified a compound with a useful potassium-sparing profile rather than merely optimizing delivery. In the separate pyrazine account, substitutions in a monocyclic series developed the synthetic-intermediate screening lead into amiloride; the pteridine and pyrazine architectures differ.

circumstances.description: The pteridine diuretic screen was planned after the kidney clue; the pyrazine effect came from routine screening. The inventors' patent also describes its reported pteridine actions as unexpected, while assigning an early aldosterone-blocking explanation. This does not establish that the initial kidney-growth observation or the entire program was accidental.

classes.name: 4-aminoquinoline antimalarials

starting.description: In the wider German antimalarial program, the observed antimalarial action of synthetic methylene blue supplied a lead for chemical development. Within the 4-aminoquinoline series itself, Blanchard's interview-based inspection report states that Pa 1501's antimalarial activity stimulated further exploration and development of resochin. The precise rationale for selecting the series when work began in 1929 is not established by this report.

inspiration.description: Previously observed effects of synthetic methylene blue and later antimalarial leads, especially Pa 1501, informed development. Quinine was an effective natural antimalarial and a replacement target in the wider program; Curd's proposed influence of its structure on side-chain choice is qualified as his inference, not a documented direct template for the initial 4-aminoquinoline series.

steps.description: Methylene blue's observed antimalarial activity became a starting point for the broader German synthetic-antimalarial program; quinine was an effective natural treatment and an intended substitute target.
Researchers modified the dye's side chains and explored other heterocyclic nuclei, producing pamaquine, an 8-aminoquinoline pursued as a synthetic quinine substitute.

In the overlapping wider program, Blanchard reports 4-aminoquinoline work from 1929 and attributes continued exploration to antimalarial activity observed for Pa 1501 after earlier negative candidates; the date of this first positive assay is not given.

According to Blanchard, ring-substituent work on active Pa 1501 led to resochin; other accounts relate active quinoline structures to portions of the working acridine quinacrine/mepacrine. The accounts disagree about resochin's exact year.

In 1950 Surrey and Hammer reported synthesized 4-aminoquinolines including the hydroxyethyl-substituted chloroquine analogue later known as hydroxychloroquine, with avian antimalarial activity and a preliminary clinical response.

design.description: Chemists varied side chains and heterocyclic nuclei, investigated structural portions of active quinacrine, and tested ring substitutions of Pa 1501 to develop resochin. Surrey and Hammer subsequently synthesized related 4-aminoquinolines with hydroxyethyl-containing side chains. These deliberate chemical changes did not erase the observed biological leads.

circumstances.description: The reported exploration of ring substitutions around active Pa 1501 and Surrey and Hammer's later search for superior 4-aminoquinolines were planned research. This does not assert that the first detection of each biological effect was expected.

classes.name: Inactivated influenza vaccines

starting.description: The investigators explicitly linked their search for immunization to the observed infection of ferrets by virus from influenza patients. They also observed that recovered ferrets resisted reinfection and that viral preparations could elicit antibodies; later work reported antigenicity after formaldehyde inactivation.

inspiration.description: Susceptibility of ferrets to patient-derived influenza virus and acquired resistance after infection, followed by experimental immune responses to viral preparations.

steps.description: Patient-derived virus infected ferrets, motivating attempts to immunize them; the researchers also observed post-infection same-strain resistance.

In 1935 formalin-treated and living preparations induced neutralizing antibodies but failed to reliably protect ferrets under the tested conditions; in 1937 Andrewes described varying immunity with experimental injections and antigenicity after formaldehyde inactivation in mice.
Andrewes's team selected formalin-inactivated virus for preliminary human vaccination and reported antibody responses without established clinical efficacy.

A 1943 human challenge study, reported in 1945, tested an egg-grown and formalin-inactivated A/B vaccine and found greater resistance to induced influenza A in vaccinated groups, with an explicit natural-disease limitation.

A separate 1943 field study of a formalin-inactivated A/B vaccine in an Army training unit reported fewer hospitalizations for its specified influenza outcome among vaccine recipients; it dates this particular field trial, not all early military vaccination.
A later surface-antigen approach selected and purified HA and NA from inactivated virus, with a historical aluminium-hydroxide formulation intended to enhance antigenicity.
A later trivalent inactivated subunit example used MF59 adjuvant; it should not be conflated with the 1976 aluminium-hydroxide preparation.

design.description: Investigators chose injection routes and prepared chemically inactivated viral antigen; later researchers purified surface HA and NA and added aluminium hydroxide to address loss of antigenicity. MF59 represents a distinct later adjuvant example.

circumstances.description: The reported vaccination and inactivation experiments were purposeful attempts to induce immunity; this does not characterize every earlier observation.

limits: The assigned class combines adjuvanted and non-adjuvanted inactivated trivalent presentations. This is a founding class history, not a demonstration of the exact genealogy or formulation of each cohort product.

Aluminium hydroxide in the 1976 account and MF59 in the review's dated 2019–2020 example are distinct historical formulation examples, not interchangeable or universal components.
Live-virus vaccines and the live challenge virus are distinct from the inactivated-vaccine class; this record does not purport to reconstruct every live or recombinant-only vaccine branch.
conflicts: A 2016 review (S5, E17) attributes protection of US military forces to Francis and Salk in 1938, while the original Salk, Menke and Francis report (S6, E18) dates one Army-program field study to 1943. gaps: The 1933 original report of virus transmission to ferrets was cited in the 1935 report but was not independently reopened. The 1935 original was read on pp. 291–294, not in its entirety.

The 1943 Henle report, 1944 preliminary challenge and field reports, and earlier surface-antigen association reports cited by the read papers were not independently reopened.

The first subunit-vaccine priority and exact manufacturing lineages of the two cohort presentations were not established; the 1976 preparation and later MF59 example are illustrative rather than exhaustive.

classes.name: Insulins and insulin analogues

starting.description: Pancreatectomy-induced diabetes localized a crucial antidiabetic function to the pancreas and motivated a search for its internal secretion. Banting describes Baron's observation of duct obstruction as the immediate stimulus for a ligation-and-extraction plan, which the team tested in diabetic dogs.

inspiration.description: Experimental pancreatic diabetes, observed responses to pancreatic duct obstruction, and a hypothesized endogenous pancreatic secretion led investigators to make extracts from animal pancreas.

steps.description: Experiments and observations linked pancreatic loss to diabetes, initiating a search for an internal secretion and its antidiabetic effects.
Toronto researchers obtained active pancreatic extracts in diabetic dogs; Collip worked on purification for human administration, with clinical responses reported in 1922.
Biosynthetic human insulin and amino-acid engineering created rapid-acting and longer-acting analogues of the known active hormone, with distinct approaches to controlling absorption and duration.

design.description: Investigators devised extraction and purification, then recombinant manufacture and insulin-sequence or acylation modifications. Rapid-acting analogues reduce self-association; long-acting analogues use slower depot release or multihexamer formation and albumin binding. These target pharmacokinetics while retaining an established insulin template and activity.

circumstances.description: The Toronto ligation and extraction experiments were deliberately planned to obtain the putative antidiabetic secretion, regardless of whether the initial ligation hypothesis was correct.

classes.name: Triazine anticonvulsants

starting.description: Researchers observed that several established anticonvulsants affected patient folate measures, while folate derivatives could provoke seizures under particular experimental conditions. These findings led to an antifolate–antiepileptic hypothesis. According to later accounts, Wellcome investigated existing synthetic antifolates including pyrimethamine, found anticonvulsant activity, and used related chemistry to search for a better antiseizure agent. The hypothesis is not established as lamotrigine's eventual mechanism.

inspiration.description: The biological clue was the observed folate–seizure relationship, including folate reductions in patients taking earlier synthetic anticonvulsants and experimentally induced convulsions with folate derivatives. Wellcome then developed from a reported anticonvulsant effect of the synthetic antifolate pyrimethamine. Folate biology, the effects of earlier compounds, the testable hypothesis, and later chemistry are distinct sources of context.

steps.description: Clinical folate changes during treatment with older anticonvulsants and experimental convulsant effects of folate derivatives contributed to the proposed antifolate–antiepileptic relationship.

In 1973 Wellcome-affiliated Baxter and Miller with Webster investigated folic acid's convulsant action while explicitly referring to the antifolate hypothesis; a later account says Wellcome examined existing antifolates including pyrimethamine for anticonvulsant effects. The precise order within 1973 is not established here.

The historical development account describes a series of structurally related phenyltriazines, including BW 288U, and further optimization to lamotrigine with weak antifolate activity; its account does not by itself verify the priority of every intermediate.

A Wellcome patent application published in 1981 describes preparation of the 2,3-dichlorophenyl triazine and anticonvulsant tests of the series. A 1986 report identifies that structure as lamotrigine and describes testing in mice and rats.

design.description: Researchers synthesized and screened structurally related phenyltriazines to improve anticonvulsant activity, changing the phenyl substitution pattern within the series. The resulting lamotrigine was a synthetic triazine with weak antifolate activity. The patent provides a specific preparation and animal tests; it does not show that weaker antifolate activity was deliberately engineered as the goal or that prior triazine chemistry was invented from scratch.

circumstances.description: The event classified here is the deliberate antifolate-hypothesis-directed testing and synthesis of analogue anticonvulsants. Cohen retrospectively called lamotrigine's discovery accidental as well, but did not specify the chance event; the discovery as a whole is therefore not assigned a more precise unexpected stage on this evidence.

classes.name: Prostaglandin analogues for glaucoma

starting.description: An unexpected sustained pressure reduction after control glass beads and accompanying ocular inflammation led Carl Camras to hypothesize a prostaglandin-mediated pressure decrease and investigate its therapeutic potential; the bead mechanism remained hypothetical.

inspiration.description: A pressure fall accompanying experimental ocular inflammation suggested a possible role for endogenous prostaglandins. Subsequent observations of pressure lowering by administered prostaglandins in rabbits and primates supplied the functional basis for the therapeutic development program.

steps.description: A sustained fall in pressure after control beads prompted an inflammation/prostaglandin hypothesis and further study.
In conscious rabbits, topical prostaglandins produced prolonged pressure decreases, sometimes after an initial rise; the authors proposed therapeutic use of PGs or analogues for ocular hypertension.
Prostaglandins also reduced ocular pressure in primates. The developer describes this prolonged effect as motivating the Columbia-Pharmacia glaucoma program.
PGF2alpha was converted to an isopropyl ester prodrug, improving bioavailability, but irritation and hyperemia remained obstacles to wider use.

Structure-activity testing yielded an unexpectedly favorable phenyl-substituted lead in animal assays; additional omega-chain and stereochemical changes produced PhXA34 and latanoprost, which entered clinical trials.

design.description: Researchers esterified PGF2alpha to improve bioavailability and then deliberately modified the omega chain to retain hypotensive activity while improving the irritation and receptor profile. The phenyl substituent, saturation of the 13,14 double bond, and selection of the 15R epimer changed the active analogue as well as its pharmacological and stability properties; this was not merely a delivery change.

circumstances.description: The control-bead pressure reduction and the cat-assay profile of a later phenyl-substituted lead were unexpected findings; the subsequent prostaglandin hypothesis, esterification and structure-activity program were deliberate investigations.

classes.name: SV2A ligands

starting.description: The decisive class-founding clue was seizure protection by the synthetic compound levetiracetam in routine screening of sound-sensitive mice; the original investigators say this finding led to wider animal testing. The earlier pyrrolidone ancestry includes a GABA-analogue sleep project and piracetam's observed psychotropic properties; piracetam's clinical myoclonus activity separately supported interest in epilepsy.

inspiration.description: The class-opening signal was the seizure-protective effect of synthetic levetiracetam in a biological mouse model. Piracetam's clinical myoclonus activity separately supported epilepsy interest. GABA was the analogue reference for the upstream piracetam sleep project, not an identified SV2A template or an established explanation of levetiracetam's antiseizure effect.

steps.description: A GABA-analogue sleep project yielded piracetam with a different psychotropic profile; later interest encouraged successor work. Its ethyl analogue was synthesized in 1966 and the S-enantiomer separated in 1977, according to S1. The specific date of discovery is disputed, and the 1966 synthesis cannot have been caused by the 1972 naming of the nootropic concept.

Routine screening showed levetiracetam seizure protection in sound-sensitive mice and led to testing in a wider range of animal models; the retrospective also identifies piracetam's clinical myoclonus activity as supporting epilepsy interest.
In a collaborator's retrospective, the audiogenic and other results led to 1989 commissioning of further kindled-rat work; the authors report clinical development and FDA approval in 1999.

Levetiracetam's brain binding site was subsequently identified as SV2A in the 2004 original report. A high-affinity ligand program built on the already observed levetiracetam effect and binding site; the exact date of its launch is not established here.

design.description: Researchers synthesized and separated pyrrolidone analogues and later pursued higher-affinity selective ligands based on the observed levetiracetam binding site.

circumstances.description: The particular tested event was a routine, deliberately performed screen in seizure-susceptible mice; the original report does not establish whether its positive result was unexpected.

classes.name: Thyroid hormone preparations

starting.description: Myxoedema-like symptoms after thyroid loss and reported effects of animal and human thyroid grafts supplied the rationale for replacing the missing gland's function with thyroid extract; both the Portuguese graft authors' proposal and Murray's later account express the graft-to-injection reasoning.

inspiration.description: Observed clinical effects of thyroid loss and animal and human graft outcomes led to the proposal to replace missing function with natural sheep thyroid extract. Thyroxine, the endogenous substance later isolated and chemically studied, was not yet identified at the original intervention.

steps.description: Clinical comparisons linked thyroid loss with myxoedema-like illness; animal thyroid-region graft experiments were reported to lessen consequences of removal, although some early grafts included parathyroid tissue.

After reporting rapid improvement from a human sheep-thyroid graft, Bettencourt and Serrano proposed that absorbed gland juice explained the effect and suggested injections in another patient; the translated excerpt records the proposal, not an injection's completion.

After discussing thyroid grafts and the proposed absorption of gland juice, Murray reasoned that injections of sheep thyroid extract could replace the missing function, and reported an improved patient. Priority for human injections is contested.
Other clinicians reported oral use of sheep thyroid or extract, and Murray later moved to oral extract administration.

A thyroid substance was later crystallized. Harington and Barger described synthesis of thyroxine and compared it chemically with gland-derived material; an appended note reported physiological observations in two patients.

In 1928 Harington described synthetic dl-thyroxine and work toward separating optical forms. In 1930 Harington and Salter obtained thyroid-derived thyroxine by enzyme treatment and found that its optical rotation agreed with synthetic l-thyroxine. A historical review discusses subsequent therapeutic use of L-thyroxine, without establishing the exact chronology of commercial products here.

design.description: Investigators grafted thyroid tissue, prepared thyroid extracts and adapted administration from injection to oral use; later they isolated a crystalline thyroid substance, synthesized thyroxine, tested its properties, separated optical forms and used enzyme treatment and optical comparisons to clarify the natural L form. The initial synthesis must not be assumed to be stereochemically pure L-thyroxine.

circumstances.description: Bettencourt and Serrano's proposed injection and Murray's trial of sheep-thyroid extract were deliberate applications of graft and gland-replacement observations; this does not characterize all earlier findings.

classes.name: DPP-4 inhibitors

starting.description: After GLP-1 had been observed to stimulate insulin secretion and show therapeutic promise, investigators identified DPP-4-mediated cleavage of GLP-1 and GIP in enzyme and serum experiments. In the Sandoz account this observation prompted a proposal to inhibit DPP-4 and preserve physiological incretin action.

inspiration.description: Endogenous GLP-1's insulin-related physiology and its experimentally observed enzymatic cleavage inspired DPP-4 inhibition in the documented programs. The same experiments showed cleavage of GIP; the Sandoz account predicted that inhibition could also protect GIP. Merck additionally cited clinical observations of glucose lowering by administered GLP-1. The therapeutic inhibitors were deliberately developed small molecules, not required to share the hormones' chemical structures.

steps.description: In purified-enzyme and human-serum experiments DPP-4 cleaved GLP-1 and GIP, and enzyme inhibitors prevented production of serum cleavage fragments.

According to the Sandoz/Novartis account the enzyme observation prompted a proposal to inhibit DPP-4 to preserve physiological GLP-1; an existing inhibitor was evaluated and optimized into DPP-728 and vildagliptin.
A 2002 four-week placebo-controlled human study reported improved glucose control with DPP-728; it was not designed to establish the mechanism of benefit.

In a parallel program begun in 1999, Merck used prior human GLP-1 and animal inhibitor evidence to choose the target, screened active compounds, and optimized a piperazine-related series into sitagliptin.

A separate program screened for DPP-4 inhibition and optimized an active xanthine scaffold into BI 1356, linagliptin, representing a different chemical route within the established incretin-protection concept.

design.description: Researchers screened and optimized small-molecule inhibitors, creating chemically distinct inhibitors including DPP-728, sitagliptin and xanthine-based linagliptin. In the sitagliptin series they introduced fused piperazine replacements to address metabolism and later improved oral absorption; in the linagliptin series they changed substituents to improve potency and reduce hERG-channel and M1-receptor interactions. These chemical inventions do not erase the observation-led target rationale.

circumstances.description: The Sandoz team's selection and testing of valine pyrrolidide as a DPP-4 inhibitor was a purposeful test of the incretin-protection hypothesis; this does not characterize every earlier observation as planned or unexpected.

classes.name: Polyethylene-glycol osmotic laxatives

cohortEntries.name: macrogol 3350 + potassium chloride + sodium bicarbonate + sodium chloride

starting.description: Prior large-volume lavage caused diarrhea and cleared the bowel but could produce a significant salt and water load. In developing a better-balanced lavage, the team selected nonabsorbable PEG over an existing mannitol osmotic agent after an observed lack of hydrogen production when PEG was incubated with fecal suspensions was communicated to them. Later, a clinical investigator attributes the move to low-volume chronic-constipation treatment to the known properties of PEG and successful bowel-cleansing use; a 1990 study explicitly tested the existing lavage as a treatment for constipation.

inspiration.description: Observed intestinal salt and water handling, the functional precedent of mannitol-based osmotic lavage, the behavior of synthetic PEG in fecal incubation and its nonabsorption, and later clinical bowel-cleansing experience. The original choice of PEG is explicitly attributed to its reported properties; the underlying Levitt test was a personal communication.

steps.description: The team investigated salt and water absorption from established lavage and designed an electrolyte solution to limit these shifts, initially using mannitol as a nonabsorbable osmotic solute.

To avoid the hydrogen-generating fermentation risk of mannitol, the team deliberately substituted PEG, basing the selection on its nonabsorption and a communicated fecal-incubation observation. They tested a high-PEG solution for minimal net fluid and electrolyte movement.

In 1989, PEG 3350 was used to induce osmotic diarrhea in healthy volunteers; increasing measured doses increased stool water output. This is a later physiological demonstration of the cohort polymer's activity, not evidence of a low-dose constipation trial or of the initial selection in 1980.

A 1990 placebo-controlled crossover study tested an existing PEG-electrolyte lavage solution, already used for bowel cleansing, as a daily treatment in patients with chronic constipation. Only the abstract was accessible; it reports five-day treatment periods and does not identify PEG molecular weight.

A later clinical investigator reports that the combination of PEG's known properties and evidence from bowel cleansing led to smaller daily volumes for treating chronic constipation, a change in purpose and dosing from a single large lavage.

design.description: The investigators combined a sulfate-based, electrolyte-adjusted lavage with an osmotically equivalent dose of PEG instead of mannitol and studied intestinal fluid and electrolyte flux. Later development adapted prior bowel-cleansing experience to lower-volume daily chronic-constipation treatment, changing both intended use and dose. These deliberate steps were built on observed physiology and properties of existing substances, not evidence of a newly designed PEG molecular scaffold.

circumstances.description: The 1980 development and testing of a nonabsorbed, low-fermentation PEG-containing lavage solution was deliberate; the source does not establish the circumstances of the original Levitt observation.

conflicts: E6: The 2025 retrospective calls the author's 1996 eight-week study the first randomized controlled trial. E7: a 1990 abstract already reports a randomized, placebo-controlled crossover trial of PEG-electrolyte lavage for chronic constipation. classes.name: Direct intestinal antispasmodics

starting.description: The starting working substance was natural reserpine, known for sedative and blood-pressure-lowering effects. Kralt and colleagues hypothesized roles for parts of its structure; their institution describes a planned synthesis of analogues to investigate the relation between structure and physiological effects. Connell later identified mebeverine as one of the phenylethylamine derivatives of reserpine, with a different, papaverine-like spasmolytic profile in animals. The exact decision to pursue intestinal spasmolysis is not documented in the accessible founding account.

inspiration.description: Previously observed physiological effects of the natural alkaloid reserpine informed a structural-analogue program; Connell's later account links that program to mebeverine. Papaverine was an established functional comparator and is also described as a structural-family analogue in a historical review, but its role as the initiating template is not established.

steps.description: Using the known pharmacology of reserpine as a starting point, the team considered which molecular groups might explain its effects; an institutional digest describes making selected analogues to examine structure and physiological activity.

Connell's 1965 account attributes to Kralt and colleagues animal findings that phenylethylamine analogues had little of reserpine's central action but marked papaverine-like spasmolytic effects, and places mebeverine among these compounds. This is Connell's secondary report, not a direct reading of the founding animal experiments.

The compound was taken into evaluation for intestinal spasm: Connell tested human colonic motility and conducted an early controlled clinical study; the inventors later disclosed a method and formulations for colonic spasm and referred to a parent preparation patent.

design.description: Researchers deliberately synthesized analogues that retained or represented selected reserpine-related chemical groups, including a phenylethylamine series, and developed a compound with a different pharmacological profile into a colonic antispasmodic. The later patent described therapeutic compositions. The exact synthetic path and the choice of individual mebeverine from the series were not verified in the inaccessible original papers.

circumstances.description: The particular documented planned event is the synthesis and study of reserpine analogues to explore structure and physiological effects. Whether the animal spasmolytic finding or its intestinal use was initially intended or unexpected is not established.

classes.name: Melatonin receptor agonists

starting.description: Bovine pineal extract lightened frog tadpole skin; researchers used the observed effect as a bioassay to isolate the responsible endogenous substance, melatonin. Later observations of nighttime melatonin and sleep-related effects helped motivate therapeutic investigation.

inspiration.description: An animal skin-pigment response to pineal extracts led to isolation of the endogenous hormone melatonin; observations of its nighttime rhythm and sleep-related effects informed subsequent therapeutic investigation.

steps.description: An observed frog-skin response to bovine pineal extract supplied a bioassay used to isolate melatonin; the investigators used synthetic material to test its proposed structure.
Pigment-cell pharmacology informed receptor hypotheses and subsequently mammalian receptor cloning.

Observations of nighttime hormone levels and earlier high-dose effects informed a deliberate low-dose human study; an investigator proposed possible use for people with low secretion. Later development included a prolonged-release hormone formulation.

Medicinal chemists prepared hormone-related analogues and replaced its indole core in other agonists; a program synthesized and optimized a constrained indan series, producing the clinical candidate TAK-375.

design.description: Investigators synthesized the identified hormone to test its structure. Later work developed prolonged-release hormone and chemically distinct agonists, including indole-core replacement and conformational restriction to alter receptor-binding and metabolic properties. The complete sequence of predecessors in the indan program is not established by the 2002 abstract.

circumstances.description: The named events are the low-dose oral-melatonin versus placebo physiology experiment and the synthesis of a receptor-active indan series; this does not characterize the chance status of every earlier finding.

classes.name: NMDA receptor antagonists (adamantane branch)

starting.description: A reported, unexpected improvement of Parkinson symptoms during antiviral amantadine use opened CNS medicinal-chemistry work on adamantanes; the known CNS-active drug became a comparator in testing the already synthesized dimethyl analogue. The sources do not explicitly establish that the individual patient case prompted the inventors' selection of that analogue.

inspiration.description: Observed clinical Parkinson effects of the synthetic antiviral amantadine and comparative biological effects of its existing synthetic dimethyl analogue. The clinical case is a family-level historical starting point; the specific reason Merz selected the analogue is not documented by these accounts.

steps.description: Before the Parkinson case, an Eli Lilly program prepared the dimethyl compound as an intermediate in work on a potential hypoglycemic sulfonylurea; the compound itself lacked the sought blood-sugar effect.
A patient's unexpected improvement while receiving antiviral amantadine was followed by clinical investigation and, according to a later history, a CNS medicinal-chemistry line involving adamantanes.

In an anti-Parkinson CNS investigation, the patent reported comparative animal effects for the already available dimethyl analogue and known active amino-adamantane. The 1978 U.S. document claims 1972 and 1973 priorities; the 1972 German filing's experimental contents have not been independently checked.

The 1999 retrospective connects preclinical NMDA findings with a 1989 application for cerebral ischemia and Alzheimer dementia; researchers later characterized the existing compound's channel-blocking kinetics. Some studies cited by that retrospective postdate 1989 and cannot have motivated that filing.

design.description: Chemists had prepared an aminoadamantane bearing two extra methyl groups for a different program. Investigators later prepared and compared its hydrochloride with known CNS-active aminoadamantane, pursued a CNS use, and later researchers characterized its NMDA channel-blocking behavior and implications of the two methyl groups. The sources do not establish that the original methyl substitutions were designed for NMDA antagonism.

circumstances.description: The clinical Parkinson response reported during amantadine influenza prevention was unexpected; the patent's comparative CNS experiments on the known compounds were planned. This does not assert that the first observation of the dimethyl analogue's CNS effects was accidental.

classes.name: Aminosalicylates

starting.description: A 1989 colleague's retrospective reports that Svartz noticed a similarity between affected tissue in rheumatoid arthritis and ulcerative colitis, prompting her to test the arthritis drug salazopyrin in colitis; this reported motive is not confirmed in the 1942 passages read. Her contemporaneous account records variable clinical improvement with sulfapyridine and, later, salazopyrin in colitis. The established effect of the parent compound then prompted investigation of its components; the observed activity of 5-aminosalicylic acid (5-ASA) informed development of targeted oral 5-ASA delivery.

inspiration.description: The retrospective tissue-similarity account supplies a reported biological observation for testing the parent drug in colitis; the primary report documents clinical responses to sulfapyridine and to the chemically assembled sulfasalazine. Existing aspirin response in arthritis contributed to the parent drug's earlier design, while the experimentally observed intestinal activity of 5-ASA guided later delivery design. These sources do not establish a shared tissue mechanism or require the active molecule to have been isolated from nature.

steps.description: For rheumatoid polyarthritis, Svartz first tried separate salicyl and sulfanilamide preparations without tangible results, then pursued chemical combinations with Pharmacia chemists. A later review describes the existing aspirin response and an infectious hypothesis as the rationale for this parent-drug design.

A colleague later attributed the choice to test salazopyrin in ulcerative colitis to Svartz's observation of apparently similar diseased tissue in the two conditions. Independently of that recollection, Svartz's 1942 report describes earlier sulfapyridine treatment of colitis and subsequent, variable responses to salazopyrin; the reports do not establish whether the earlier sulfapyridine response caused the initial salazopyrin trial.

With sulfasalazine already used for ulcerative colitis, the 1977 blinded enema comparison tested the parent and its two cleavage products. The authors identified 5-ASA as the active intestinal moiety; the original report was accessible as an abstract and its historical role is also described in the full-text review.

A 1982 report cited the component experiment, explained why uncoated oral 5-ASA needed a colonic delivery system, and tested an acrylic-coated formulation for remission maintenance. Its reported nonsignificant relapse difference from sulfasalazine in a short trial does not by itself establish equivalence.

The established class includes unlinked mesalazine delivered in delayed- or slow-release formulations; another later approach linked two 5-ASA molecules to deliver the active moiety without sulfapyridine. These are delivery adaptations of the intestinal lineage, not independent starting points asserted for each analogue.

design.description: Researchers deliberately linked a salicylate and sulfonamide for an arthritis program, later tested which cleavage product supplied intestinal activity, and designed coated or otherwise modified delivery of the observed active 5-ASA without the original sulfapyridine carrier. The later colonic-delivery rationale must not be projected back onto the original arthritis design.

circumstances.description: The chemical-combination program, the tissue-motivated colitis test as retrospectively described, and the later coated formulation were planned actions. Svartz characterized the speed of response in one case as difficult to explain, while a later review described colitis improvement as unexpected. Neither account establishes that trying the drug in colitis was accidental.

classes.name: Biguanide glucose-lowering agents

starting.description: Observed glucose-lowering effects of guanidine-related compounds and prior galegine experience, alongside flumamine evidence and purposeful follow-up testing, informed the later development of a useful biguanide therapy. The disputed influenza-patient measurement remains unresolved.

inspiration.description: Galegine and other guanidine-related glucose-lowering observations informed the historical context; the later selection also used experimental effects of synthetic biguanides and prior flumamine experience.

steps.description: Guanidine and plant-associated galegine were reported to lower glucose, with galegine and synthalin trialed therapeutically before toxicity limited their use. A 1928 experimental article describes further comparative animal investigation of guanidine derivatives prompted by the prior observations.
A parallel chemical history yielded biguanides; metformin and other biguanides were reported to lower glucose in animal studies in 1929.
Sterne and Duval reassessed the flumamine and galegine history, studied several compounds in animals, and selected metformin for clinical investigation; Sterne reported diabetes treatment in 1957.

Other groups investigated guanidine derivatives in the 1950s; contemporary phenformin and buformin reports illustrate parallel work within the class, without establishing each group's motivating clue here.

design.description: Researchers synthesized and compared guanidine-related biguanides, tested their glucose-lowering activity and tolerability, and selected metformin for clinical development; the individual historical synthesis papers remain to be checked.

circumstances.description: Sterne and Duval's comparative animal investigation and selection of metformin for diabetes studies were purposeful; this does not characterize the initial finding of every preceding observation.

classes.name: Carbamate skeletal muscle relaxants

starting.description: Existing glycerol ethers had observed skeletal-muscle-relaxant effects: Berger and Bradley documented the related mephenesin effect, while the glyceryl guaiacolate parent of methocarbamol was also described as muscle-relaxing. Murphey explicitly used these known active compounds as the prior-art context for a new carbamate.

inspiration.description: Previously observed muscle-relaxing activity of related glycerol ethers, including mephenesin and glyceryl guaiacolate; the latter was the chemical parent of methocarbamol. An existing mephenesin carbamate was also prior art. No claim is made that a natural material motivated the program.

steps.description: Following observed muscle relaxation in a glycerol-ether series, Berger and Bradley selected myanesin for pharmacological and preliminary clinical evaluation.

By 1951 Ginzel had compared the related myanesin with Myokain, o-methoxyphenyl glycerol ether, for central paralytic and anticonvulsant effects, among other properties. A later contemporary account identifies the glyceryl guaiacolate parent of methocarbamol as muscle relaxing.

Murphey described prior active glycerol-ether relaxants and proposed an ortho-alkoxy-substituted carbamate series, including the glyceryl-guaiacolate carbamate, to seek improved duration and reduced adverse hemolytic action.
A 1958 pharmacological comparison identified AHR-85 as methocarbamol and reported longer protection for the carbamate than its glycerol-ether parent in a rat strychnine-challenge assay.

design.description: Murphey carbamylated the terminal hydroxyl of an active glycerol-ether parent, using an ortho-alkoxy-substituted aromatic structure, with the stated goals of prolonging activity and reducing adverse hemolytic action. This is deliberate structural optimization of active leads, not evidence of a de novo therapeutic concept.

circumstances.description: The specific event described as planned is Murphey's carbamate-development objective; whether the initial observation of relaxation was unexpected is not established by the cited original study.

classes.name: Antifolate antimetabolites

starting.description: Farber's interpretation of apparent leukemia acceleration after folate conjugates, experience with folate deficiency, and observed growth inhibition by a synthetic folate antagonist suggested testing more powerful antagonists. His 1947 report traces the earlier conjugate trials to mouse-tumor studies that Diamond later said could not be substantiated. These historical observations are not proof of a causal acceleration effect.

inspiration.description: The natural vitamin folate, interpreted clinical and physiological effects, and an observed synthetic folate antagonist's growth effects in experimental organisms supplied clues for the cancer program.

steps.description: Prior mouse reports prompted folate-conjugate trials; folate-related clinical observations and measured biological antagonism suggested testing folate antagonists against rapidly growing malignancies. An early pteroylaspartic-acid observation helped motivate stronger antagonists.
Chemists synthesized a potent 4-amino folate antagonist by 1947; aminopterin was tested in children with leukemia, with temporary improvements and important toxicity.

Amethopterin, later methotrexate, was developed and tested as another folate antagonist; Farber's 1949 abstract reports temporary remissions and toxicity with it. It is the N10-methyl analogue of aminopterin.

design.description: Chemists synthesized folate analogues and measured antagonistic activity. Aminopterin has an amino substitution in place of the pteridine oxygen, and methotrexate has an additional N10-methyl group; these are changes in active structure, not merely formulation. Clinical investigators deliberately tested the antagonists against leukemia following biological and clinical clues.

circumstances.description: The testing of folate antagonists in children with leukemia was a deliberate therapeutic investigation; this does not classify every earlier observation as planned or accidental.

classes.name: Nitroimidazole antibacterials

starting.description: A naturally produced antibiotic, azomycin, was observed to have antimicrobial and later antitrichomonal activity. According to the 1978 history, this observed lead stimulated the preparation and testing of accessible 5-nitroimidazole isomers. A separate 1956 laboratory experiment directly reported azomycin's antitrichomonal effect, without establishing which experiment motivated the French program.

inspiration.description: The first lead was natural azomycin and its observed activity against microorganisms, including Trichomonas. A separate later observation of clinical benefit in gingivitis motivated antibacterial follow-up of the synthetic medicine.

steps.description: Azomycin was obtained from microbial culture and identified as 2-nitroimidazole; its bacteriostatic activity was experimentally examined.

Recognizing antitrichomonal activity in azomycin supplied a lead for the preparation and testing of accessible 5-nitroimidazoles; metronidazole was selected from a series for its activity-to-toxicity balance and introduced for trichomoniasis. Horie's separate 1956 experiment directly documented the natural lead's antitrichomonal activity.
A clinical gingivitis observation attributed to Shinn in 1962 motivated a 1964 study of 15 patients; the investigators also examined the compound against oral spirochetes and a Bacteroides strain.

By 1972 investigators had tested metronidazole against anaerobic and microaerophilic isolates and reported initial treatment of anaerobic infections, while emphasizing that this use remained experimental. A later editorial describes its establishment for anaerobic infections.

design.description: Researchers prepared and tested more accessible 5-nitroimidazoles related to the natural 2-nitroimidazole lead and selected the hydroxyethyl-substituted metronidazole for its balance of activity and toxicity; this was a positional and substituent change, not merely a delivery modification.

circumstances.description: Preparation and testing of the synthetic 5-nitroimidazole series was planned; the distinct clinical observation that directed attention to gingivitis was described as incidental and prompted a deliberate follow-up study.

classes.name: Beta3-adrenoceptor agonists

starting.description: The early metabolic programs sought to retain the already observed thermogenic and antiobesity effects of nonselective sympathomimetics in rodents while avoiding other beta-mediated effects. Adipocyte studies exposed an atypical receptor later identified with beta3. Separately, sympathetic stimulation was known to relax bladder muscle; human bladder experiments implicated beta3, motivating the overactive-bladder application. For the specific Astellas chemical series, the chemist reports starting from a different, already human-beta3-active Merck compound after unsuccessful work on early rodent-active leads.

inspiration.description: Observed sympathomimetic effects and adipocyte pharmacology supplied the metabolic clue; the bladder clue was a sympathetic physiological relationship involving endogenous noradrenaline and later beta3-active compounds in human tissue. The eventual Astellas lead was an already human-beta3-active synthetic compound. These descriptions do not claim mirabegron was isolated from a natural source or that its scaffold was copied from noradrenaline.

steps.description: In the late 1970s and early 1980s, companies deliberately sought to retain rodent thermogenic and antiobesity effects of nonselective sympathomimetics while reducing cardiac and tremor effects.

Beecham identified agonists acting on atypical rodent adipocyte receptors; subsequent receptor work established the beta3 context for metabolic research. The contemporary 1984 report's abstract describes selective brown-adipocyte lipolysis.

The Astellas program aimed to find a type 2 diabetes treatment. After early rodent-active compounds proved difficult to improve for human use, it initiated a new series from a Merck-disclosed human-beta3 agonist and designed an active phenylacetanilide lead.

The team modified the acetanilide and then substantially changed the phenoxy-containing portion to a phenylethanolamine series, measuring human subtype potency and selectivity and optimizing further. The discoverer traces the series to a 2-aminothiazole analogue selected as mirabegron.

Independently, bladder physiology and 1999 experiments on human detrusor implicated beta3 in relaxation. The Astellas pharmacologists explicitly say this physiological evidence prompted research into beta3 agonism for overactive bladder; this step is not asserted to have occurred after every chemical step above.

The chemist reports inadequate effectiveness in a type 2 diabetes trial and continued development for overactive bladder. The pharmacologists report animal and human bladder experiments followed by clinical studies; the 2007 original report's abstract independently describes YM178 testing in bladder strips.

design.description: Researchers deliberately sought improved subtype selectivity and human activity, designed a phenylacetanilide based on an already active synthetic agonist, replaced a phenoxy-containing portion with phenylethanolamine architecture, and modified heterocyclic and other groups. They assessed potency, beta1/beta2 selectivity, pharmacokinetics and physical properties when advancing the series to mirabegron. These were substantive changes in structure and activity, not just delivery optimization or a design without an observed functional starting point.

circumstances.description: The selective metabolic-drug search, human-active lead development and subsequent investigation of beta3 agonism for bladder treatment were planned research stages. This does not assert that all individual experimental results were anticipated or exclude unreported chance events.

classes.name: Noradrenergic and specific serotonergic antidepressants

starting.description: Peet and Behagel report an unexpected possible mood-lifting effect of mianserin in some subjects, followed by an EEG comparison and clinical investigation. Leonard recalls a route from observed sedation to EEG prediction; Fink emphasizes the EEG finding, and Itil attributes discovery of clinical antidepressant effects solely to that method. The respective contributions remain disputed. Organon later continued the tetracyclic series and selected mirtazapine as a potential anxiolytic antidepressant.

inspiration.description: Accounts variously emphasize subjective mood or sedative effects and an observed human EEG profile of the synthetic compound mianserin; the relative initiating roles are disputed.

steps.description: The 1969 human mood observation followed synthesis and testing in an anti-5-HT program.

Human EEG comparisons and subsequent pilot clinical studies investigated antidepressant potential. The institutional account describes EEG as following the mood clue; Fink and Itil give the EEG a more central role, while Leonard describes sedation before EEG prediction.
Organon continued its tetracyclic series and selected mirtazapine as a potential anxiolytic antidepressant; Pinder says that the effect on serotonin release was recognized later.
In 1982, investigators compared the 6-aza mianserin analogue Org 3770, which Pinder identifies as mirtazapine, with mianserin in pharmacological assays.
By the 1996 interview, Pinder reported that mirtazapine was approved and marketed in the United States.

design.description: Pinder retrospectively describes an earlier anti-allergy structural design using cyproheptadine and phenbenzamine as ideas. Researchers then investigated the compound's observed central effects, and continued the tetracyclic chemical series to select the 6-aza analogue mirtazapine for antidepressant development. The earlier anti-allergy design was not itself shown to be de novo antidepressant design.

circumstances.description: The mood-related observation was unexpected within the original anti-5-HT program; the subsequent EEG and clinical investigations were planned.

classes.name: Leukotriene receptor antagonists

starting.description: Observed release of SRS-A during anaphylaxis and its smooth-muscle-contracting activity motivated an early antagonist screen. Later evidence of cysteinyl leukotriene bronchoconstriction supported therapeutic antagonist programs; in the Merck quinoline series, a measured antagonist effect in a broad compound screen supplied an additional lead.

inspiration.description: Observed anaphylaxis-associated SRS-A activity motivated functional antagonist screening; the endogenous cysteinyl leukotrienes' airway effects supported further programs. Other: a compound's observed antagonist effect supplied a quinoline-series lead; the original preparation of that screen hit is not specified in the accessible original abstract.

steps.description: SRS-A release during anaphylaxis and its ability to contract smooth muscle supplied a biological starting clue for an antagonist screen.
The investigators screened their compounds against SRS-A in isolated guinea-pig ileum and used structure–activity relationships to develop antagonists including FPL 55712.

Identification and pharmacological study of cysteinyl leukotriene mediators and their bronchoconstricting effects led to a search for selective antagonists; the Merck Frosst program began by synthesizing leukotrienes and later pursued antagonists and, separately, biosynthesis inhibitors.
A separate Merck quinoline-series lead showed LTD4-antagonist activity in broad screening; researchers transformed its structure and developed an orally active antagonist, MK-571.

Medicinal-chemistry accounts trace the quinoline series through leukotriene-inspired structural modifications and development of MK-571, followed by work addressing peroxisomal enzyme induction and leading to montelukast.

design.description: Researchers developed the early SRS-A antagonist using structure–activity relationships. In the quinoline series they changed an aromatic ring and introduced or modified acidic groups, including leukotriene-inspired structural elements, to obtain a potent, orally active antagonist; subsequent work addressed peroxisomal enzyme induction. These are substantive changes in antagonist structure, activity and experimentally measured enzyme induction, not merely delivery optimization.

circumstances.description: The SRS-A functional antagonist screen and subsequent structure–activity work were deliberate; the abstract does not establish whether every upstream observation was anticipated.

classes.name: Pseudomonic-acid / isoleucyl-tRNA-synthetase inhibitors

starting.description: Investigators developed an antibacterial substance from the observed antagonistic activity of Pseudomonas fluorescens cultures: the inhibitory material was isolated and characterized as pseudomonic acid, the founding lead of the mupirocin family.

inspiration.description: Antibacterial antagonism observed in bacterial cultures led to isolation of the natural bacterial metabolite pseudomonic acid; the named 1887 observation is historical context, not proof that its active compound was identical.

steps.description: The Imperial College investigators isolated and characterized pseudomonic acid from the inhibitory products of P. fluorescens cultures, following evidence of antibacterial antagonism.
The inventors described an activity-guided isolation process: culturing a producer, removing inactive material, concentrating active fractions and separating pseudomonic acid from the mixture.
After pseudomonic acid had been isolated, investigators reported inhibition of isoleucyl-tRNA synthetase, explaining a molecular target of the established natural antibiotic.

Systemic degradation limited oral and parenteral prospects, and Beecham researchers studied the established natural antibacterial agent for topical use, including tests against clinical skin isolates.

design.description: Researchers developed an activity-guided purification process and characterized the natural antibacterial material, then developed a topical application in response to systemic degradation; the cited testimony does not establish a new designed active chemical scaffold.

circumstances.description: The 1985 antibacterial evaluation for topical use was expressly designed for that purpose. The evidence does not establish whether the original observation or choice of strain was planned or unexpected.

classes.name: Nitrofuran antibacterials

starting.description: A founding observation was that synthetic 5-nitrofuran derivatives inhibited bacterial growth, with substantially greater activity than corresponding non-nitrated furans in the reported comparisons. The Eaton researchers later described established in-vitro activity as directing attention toward treatment of systemic infection. This is an observed founding class clue; the reason the research program first chose furans in 1939 is not established.

inspiration.description: Observed bacteriostatic activity of synthetic nitrofuran compounds, particularly effects revealed by comparisons of 5-nitrated and non-nitrated furan derivatives. The later practical research was directed to developing that demonstrated activity; the source does not establish the earlier reason for choosing the chemical family.

steps.description: A retrospective reports that an Eaton Laboratories nitrofuran research program began in 1939. The reported reason for starting that program is not established by this account.

A 1944 in-vitro comparison found that nitrated furan derivatives generally inhibited bacteria more strongly than their non-nitrated counterparts; the original article is available here only through a reproduced abstract.

An Eaton laboratory report explicitly states that established in-vitro activity led to attention to possible treatment of systemic infection. Stillman and Scott described and synthesized members of an antiseptic nitrofuran family, including the semicarbazone known as nitrofurazone, and made claims of oral activity.

Additional 5-nitrofurans were selected from hundreds synthesized; Hayes described an aminohydantoin series with a preferred compound corresponding to nitrofurantoin and reported antibacterial urine in treated animals. A later account places nitrofurantoin clinical trials in 1952.

design.description: Researchers prepared and compared nitrated and non-nitrated furans, synthesized related semicarbazones, and later prepared aminohydantoin derivatives including the compound corresponding to nitrofurantoin. The later patent reports antibacterial urinary excretion in animals; the documents read do not establish that urinary persistence was rationalized in advance as the original design hypothesis.

circumstances.description: The specific documented event is a purposeful laboratory survey and comparison of antibacterial activity. The available abstract does not establish whether the observed enhancement was expected or accidental, and this value is not a blanket claim about every step.
