classes.name: Fluoroquinolone antibacterials

starting.description: The Sterling lineage is retrospectively traced to antibacterial activity of a synthetic chloroquine-synthesis by-product, distinct from later nalidixic acid. At the later Kyorin stage, the activity of existing quinolones and observed C6 structure–activity trends led researchers to create halogenated C7-piperazinyl analogues. The separate earlier ICI program's starting insight is not established.

inspiration.description: Observed antibacterial effects of synthetic compounds: the Sterling by-product and, in the later Kyorin program, working quinolone analogues and their measured structure–activity trends. The initiating insight for ICI's independent early work is unknown.

steps.description: The Sterling lineage is retrospectively traced to an antibacterially active synthetic by-product and the development of related structures including nalidixic acid; the exact intervening rationale remains unclear.
An independent ICI program disclosed antibacterial quinolones, including a C6-fluoro example, in a patent filed in 1957 and published in 1960. Its own initiating clue is not documented in the review.

Building on active quinolones, Kyorin researchers combined prior C6-halogen activity findings with C7-piperazinyl analogues, influenced also by another company's C6-methyl patent. They synthesized C6-chloro AM-700 in 1976 and the more active C6-fluoro AM-715/norfloxacin in 1977.

A contemporary study reported AM-715's antibacterial activity against tested gram-positive and gram-negative organisms, including Pseudomonas, compared with older analogues. Norfloxacin was an early drug of the C6-fluoro/C7-basic-amino combination; ofloxacin is a later member of the broad fluoroquinolone class.

design.description: Researchers deliberately synthesized and tested structural analogues, combining C6 halogens and C7 piperazinyl substituents to improve antibacterial activity and spectrum, subsequently choosing and developing a fluorinated analogue.

circumstances.description: The Kyorin team's synthesis and antibacterial testing of C6-halogen/C7-piperazinyl quinolone analogues was a deliberate development program guided by previous activity findings; this does not establish whether the earlier Sterling by-product's antibacterial effect was sought or unexpected.

conflicts: S1 distinguishes the earlier by-product from nalidixic acid in its Introduction, but section 2 calls nalidixic acid itself a by-product. S2's detailed reconstruction distinguishes the two; S1's inconsistency is not erased.
S1 calls the impurity's activity modest, whereas S2 cautions that available Sterling publications do not establish the lead's purportedly limited potency or spectrum.

S3's historical background asserts that ICI patent coverage drove Lesher toward naphthyridines, while S2 says the extent of Sterling's early awareness and its precise rationale are unknown or speculative; S3 is not a firsthand witness to that earlier event.
gaps: The 1962 Lesher report is located but not read; the 1993 Wentland memorial and 1986 Lesher symposium account were not read independently of their reproduction in S2.
ICI's initial inspiration and Sterling's exact reason for choosing the naphthyridone core are not established by the historical review; the ICI patent itself was not read.
The specific step-by-step development of each later derivative, including ofloxacin, was not reconstructed because the assigned unit is the class.

classes.name: 5-HT3 receptor antagonists

starting.description: Clinical and experimental antiemetic effects of metoclopramide, and ferret responses to renzapride versus a dopamine antagonist, prompted investigation of a non-dopaminergic mechanism. Separately, a Glaxo migraine pilot's reported nausea relief and metoclopramide's high-dose effectiveness prompted work on ondansetron as an antiemetic.

inspiration.description: Observed antiemetic effects of synthetic metoclopramide and renzapride, reported nausea relief with ondansetron in a migraine pilot, serotonin-related responses, and cocaine as a separate pharmacological and chemical starting point for the MDL72222 experimental tool; no cocaine-to-ondansetron molecular ancestry is established.

steps.description: High-dose metoclopramide reduced chemotherapy-associated emesis, motivating investigation beyond dopamine antagonism.
In a separate chemical and pharmacological branch, cocaine and related molecules supplied a starting point for MDL72222, made for a migraine research program rather than initially as an antiemetic.

Renzapride suppressed cisplatin vomiting without D2 antagonism; researchers used MDL72222 to test whether a selective serotonin-receptor antagonist was antiemetic. In the 1986 test it reduced cisplatin-induced vomiting in ferrets.

In Glaxo's parallel route, an uncontrolled 1985 ondansetron migraine pilot reportedly relieved nausea and vomiting in some patients; together with metoclopramide evidence this led Tyers to pursue a 5-HT3 antiemetic hypothesis, followed by animal and clinical development.
Glaxo's 1988 pharmacological experiments characterized ondansetron (GR38032F) as a selective 5-HT3 antagonist, and the retrospective reports subsequent U.S. registration in 1991.

design.description: Researchers synthesized the selective MDL72222 antagonist using a cocaine template and deliberately tested it after antiemetic observations. Separately, Glaxo synthesized ondansetron, characterized its selective receptor antagonism and developed it for antiemetic use. The MDL72222 template is not a proven chemical lineage for ondansetron, whose detailed design route is not established here.

circumstances.description: The follow-up experiment with the selective antagonist was planned to probe competing mechanisms; this does not characterize every earlier discovery as planned or unexpected.

sources.citation: Sanger GJ, Andrews PLR. 2018. A History of Drug Discovery for Treatment of Nausea and Vomiting and the Implications for Future Research. Front Pharmacol 9:913. DOI 10.3389/fphar.2018.00913; PMID 30233361.

The exact medicinal-chemistry route to ondansetron and precise priority among all early investigators were not established; the early Fozard migraine publication and underlying testimony in the litigation dispute were not read.

classes.name: Anilide non-opioid analgesics

starting.description: The reported antipyretic effect of synthetic acetanilide became an observed lead for research on related antipyretics, including phenacetin and the subsequent paracetamol search. A later, distinct observation that paracetamol was a prominent acetanilide metabolite in plasma prompted appraisal of its analgesic activity.

inspiration.description: An observed antipyretic effect of synthetic acetanilide, clinical response including a reported case of pain relief, and the later acetanilide-to-paracetamol metabolic relationship pertain to distinct stages; the metabolite is not described as an endogenous starting template.

steps.description: Cahn and Hepp reported antipyretic effects of acetanilide; a contemporary review describes fortunate access and subsequent tests in animals and fever patients, including a report of pain relief in one rheumatism case.

Acetanilide's success and adverse effects prompted research on related chemicals; phenacetin was prepared and tested as another antipyretic. Accounts disagree about the precise role of luck and who initiated the chemistry.

Paracetamol, described retrospectively as chemically synthesized by Morse in 1878, was assessed during the later search for alternatives to phenacetin. Von Mering reported clinical work in 1893; accounts differ about the first trial date.

Brodie and Axelrod's 1948 investigation of acetanilide metabolism found substantial N-acetyl-p-aminophenol; its high plasma concentration prompted analgesic appraisal. Flinn and Brodie's 1948 heat-radiation study reported analgesic activity.

The later metabolic findings contributed to renewed interest and market introduction of paracetamol in the 1950s; this was a later development, not its original synthesis or first clinical assessment.

design.description: Chemists prepared and pharmacologists tested related structures in pursuit of effective antipyresis with fewer adverse effects; phenacetin and paracetamol are structurally distinct compounds. The review reports that paracetamol itself had been prepared before the therapeutic search. This was a change in active chemical structure and biological testing, not merely a delivery adjustment.

circumstances.description: The early acquisition of the antipyretic preparation was described as fortunate. The subsequent search among related chemicals and the later metabolite investigation and pain-threshold appraisal were deliberate; this does not assert that every observation in the overall sequence was planned or accidental.

S1 supports the reported acetanilide effect and clinical testing, but not the detailed pharmacy anecdote. S2, S4, S5 and S6 are retrospective accounts and may share source ancestry.

The 1948 acetanilide-to-paracetamol metabolism and analgesic work is a later development/rediscovery contribution, not the chemical invention of paracetamol or its first clinical trial. The separate 1949 phenacetin metabolism report was located but not read.
The class boundary does not assert that paracetamol is a conventional peripheral NSAID, nor does this record settle its modern mechanism or prove a universal comparative safety ranking.
conflicts: S2 and S5 repeat the naphthalene/worms/pharmacy story; S4 explicitly says it cannot be substantiated. S1's near-contemporary review describes a fortunate occurrence but does not establish the detailed anecdote.

S2 reports competing accounts of whether luck or systematic chemistry was central to phenacetin's discovery; S4 describes an acetanilide-led commercial and chemical project. These differences do not negate the preceding observed acetanilide effect.

S6 dates the first reported clinical use to 1887 while citing the 1893 von Mering paper; S5 describes a trial in 1893. Without reading the primary report, a study-versus-publication distinction is possible but the earliest-use date remains unresolved.

S3's claim about how much analgesia was mediated by the metabolite is reported as its authors' historical conclusion, not independently established here.
gaps: The 1886 Cahn-Hepp original and von Mering's 1893 original were located but HathiTrust returned HTTP 403; the detailed original circumstances, exact first clinical-use date and original adverse-effect findings remain unverified.
The 1878 Morse original was identified from publisher metadata but not read; S6 is the cited retrospective source for its link to paracetamol, not proof of Morse's purpose.

Flinn and Brodie's 1948 pain-threshold article was read only as the indexed publisher abstract; the separate 1949 Brodie-Axelrod phenacetin report was not read. A proposed impurity as the explanation for von Mering's adverse-effect observation remains hypothetical.

classes.name: Sympathomimetic amine anorectics

starting.description: Weight loss observed during early clinical amphetamine use led to investigation of the drug for obesity; its demonstrated appetite-suppressing effects then supplied a functional lead for later anorectics. The identity of the first observer remains unresolved.

inspiration.description: Observed weight loss and appetite suppression associated with synthetic amphetamine use, followed by a search for related compounds retaining this effect.

steps.description: In the 1930s, clinical amphetamine use for other conditions was accompanied by reports of weight loss; Wilbur and colleagues described their observations in 1937.

The Endotext history reports that Myerson took up reports of weight loss and, with Lesses, designed an obesity trial published in 1938. Its attribution of a weight observation to the 1935 narcolepsy report is disputed.
Separately, an application filed in 1942 described synthesis of the substance later identified as phentermine in a vasopressor and low-stimulation program, not an expressly anorectic one.

The review describes a class-wide search for compounds retaining amphetamine's appetite-suppressing effect while seeking less dependence liability, and identifies phentermine as an anorectic marketed in 1959. It does not establish the specific bridge from the 1942 patent to phentermine's obesity development.

design.description: The class history describes synthesis and testing of amphetamine-related structures to retain appetite suppression while seeking reduced dependence liability. Separately, the 1942 application on the compound later called phentermine pursued a vasopressor with little central stimulation, not an expressly anorectic use. The precise bridge from that chemistry to phentermine's anorectic development remains unestablished; neither objective demonstrates that the products were free of risks.

circumstances.description: The later search for anorectic compounds retaining amphetamine's effect is described as intentional; the intent behind the first weight-loss observation is not established here.

classes.name: Thiazolidinediones

starting.description: While looking for lipid-lowering agents, Takeda observed that synthetic AL-294 also acted against hyperglycemia in diabetic yellow KK mice, then modified it to seek greater activity, yielding AL-321. In a distinct program, Sankyo hypothesized that lipid peroxides contributed to diabetic disorders and advanced CS-045 after screening and observing its biological activity.

inspiration.description: The observed glucose- and lipid-lowering effects of synthetic AL-294 supplied the working Takeda lead. In a distinct antioxidant-oriented program, tested synthetic CS-045 showed metabolic effects and was further developed; a different hypothesis does not establish design from scratch.

steps.description: During a lipid-lowering search, AL-294 showed glucose- and lipid-lowering effects in insulin-resistant diabetic yellow KK mice; its modification yielded thiazolidinedione AL-321.
AL-321 analogue studies led to ciglitazone; further studies seeking greater potency produced pioglitazone, including work on pyridylethoxy substituents.

A distinct Sankyo program tested hindered phenols for glucose/lipid effects together with antioxidant activity; a thiazolidinedione derived from another tested compound became CS-045 (troglitazone), and its observed activity supported further development.

design.description: The researchers modified active AL-294, made and tested AL-321 derivatives, and pursued increased potency, including a pyridylethoxy substitution leading toward pioglitazone. The distinct Sankyo program synthesized and screened hindered phenols for glucose/lipid effects and antioxidant activity, including a new thiazolidinedione structure.

circumstances.description: Later Takeda structure–activity studies sought a more potent compound; Sankyo planned testing for metabolic and antioxidant activities. Whether the initial AL-294 glucose effect was unexpected is not established by the primary account read.

classes.name: Potassium replacement salts

starting.description: For Darrow's pediatric potassium-replacement branch, experimental loss and restoration of cellular potassium in rats and the clinical potassium losses and response observed in a patient with congenital alkalosis and diarrhea led him to anticipate deficits in infants with diarrhea and to consider potassium administration beneficial.

inspiration.description: Observed cellular potassium depletion and response to potassium chloride in animal experiments, together with electrolyte losses and clinical observations in a patient, informed Darrow's pediatric replacement work.

steps.description: Miller and Darrow observed abnormal muscle electrolytes in potassium-depleted rats and an increase in muscle potassium after potassium chloride; Darrow acknowledged Heppel's independently reported earlier similar findings.

In a patient with congenital alkalosis and diarrhea, Darrow recorded potassium loss and improvement during treatment that included potassium chloride in feeds and saline; the 1945 original report's indexed summary describes the same patient and both salts.

Darrow later explained that this patient and the preceding physiological work made him expect potassium deficits in infants with diarrhea and supported use of potassium in their treatment, conditional on the expected deficits being present.
Govan and Darrow's 1946 report described incorporating potassium chloride into electrolyte solutions for dehydrated infants with diarrhea, applying replacement within a multi-component regimen.

In a separate earlier context, Watson attributed potassium-salt therapy for periodic paralysis to 1901–1902; by 1938 a report described potassium chloride. Later work associated attacks with redistribution and did not establish a chronic whole-body potassium deficit.

design.description: Clinicians measured and interpreted potassium losses, incorporated potassium chloride into feeds and later multi-electrolyte fluid regimens, and extended potassium administration to infants with diarrheal deficits; this was application of an existing salt, not a documented creation of a new molecule.

circumstances.description: Darrow's contemplated use of potassium in infant diarrhea was a planned application based on prior observations and an explicit expectation of potassium deficit. The account does not establish whether the original observations themselves were unexpected.

classes.name: Phenothiazine antipsychotics

starting.description: In related but not demonstrably identical strands, Rhône-Poulenc pursued observed central effects of synthetic antihistamines, while Laborit observed calming and detachment in patients given promethazine and sought a related compound; clinical chlorpromazine observations then suggested psychiatric potential. The influence of Laborit's findings on the company's initial program is disputed.

inspiration.description: Observed central effects of synthetic antihistamines, including clinical calming and detachment with promethazine; subsequent clinical effects of chlorpromazine and, in the separate antiemetic branch, inhibition of induced vomiting in dogs.

steps.description: A planned company program exploited observed central effects of synthetic antihistamines; in a related clinical strand, promethazine's calming effects prompted Laborit to request a more centrally active phenothiazine. The clinical observations' influence on the initial company program remains disputed.

Chlorpromazine was studied in surgical patients and proposed for psychiatric use; French clinical reports led to further psychiatric evaluation, including a 1954 controlled study with qualified behavioral findings.

In a parallel antiemetic line, chlorpromazine was observed to suppress apomorphine-induced vomiting in dogs, prompting further animal experiments, and was subsequently investigated as a clinical antiemetic; prochlorperazine is a piperazine-side-chain phenothiazine antiemetic.
Research on chemically related drugs followed chlorpromazine's promise; piperazine-side-chain derivatives such as prochlorperazine represented a substantive chemical and pharmacological variation.

design.description: Researchers deliberately sought phenothiazines with central effects and later investigated structural variants to improve potency and therapeutic usefulness. Piperazine-side-chain derivatives including prochlorperazine differ from chlorpromazine; specific design intent for that individual analogue is not established here.

circumstances.description: Ban characterizes Laborit's observation of promethazine-related detachment as serendipitous. The company program deliberately explored already observed central effects, and Laborit deliberately requested a related drug. Cunningham Owens cautions against treating the entire psychiatric introduction as a pure fluke; these labels concern specific stages, not every event.

classes.name: Quinoline-alkaloid antimalarials

starting.description: Medicinal use of cinchona bark and reports of its effects on intermittent fevers preceded quinine's isolation. Pelletier and Caventou explicitly investigated recognized febrifuge barks, building on earlier work on a cinchona constituent and the observation that plant bases could be active. Early historical accounts connect Indigenous medicinal knowledge and European use, but the original observer and exact transmission of antimalarial use are disputed.

inspiration.description: The medicinal natural substance was cinchona bark; the relevant biological effect was the reported interruption or reduction of intermittent fever. Prior chemical observations of plant bases and Gomes's cinchonin guided the later analytical search; this later reasoning did not originate the therapeutic target from scratch.

steps.description: Andean medicinal knowledge and early accounts of bark use against shivering and intermittent fevers preceded the chemists' work. Reviews describe different possible Indigenous and Jesuit contributions; the first use and transfer are not established.

By the early nineteenth century, positive reports of cinchona bark for intermittent fevers had accumulated. Pelletier and Caventou deliberately analyzed these already medicinal barks, prompted also by prior plant-alkali chemistry and Gomes's reported cinchonin.
In 1820, the chemists differentiated the basic constituent from yellow cinchona, named it quinine, and described obtaining and separating it from cinchonine.

Doctors then investigated the separated substance and its salts for intermittent fevers. In 1823 Elliotson reported a sulphate-treated patient's course and deliberately tested quinina itself, describing its potential as a more affordable preparation; these reports were not controlled trials.

design.description: Researchers developed chemical extraction and separation of an existing bark constituent, distinguished quinine from cinchonine, and investigated quinine and salt preparations clinically. Separating active material allowed more quantitative administration; Elliotson explicitly considered a less costly preparation. These were analytical and formulation contributions to an existing medicinal observation, not evidence of the molecule being designed from scratch.

circumstances.description: The recorded event is the deliberate 1820 investigation of cinchona constituents, with subsequent purposeful clinical testing of quinina by Elliotson. Whether the earliest discovery of bark's medicinal effect was planned or accidental is not established here.

conflicts: S1 treats the first Indigenous or Jesuit use of bark specifically for malarial fever as unresolved. S5 reviews accounts of Indigenous febrifuge use and asserts a particular transfer involving Pedro Leiva, while also presenting alternative discovery scenarios. These differing degrees of historical attribution are not resolved here; the reviews share a coauthor and historical sources.

S1 describes the quinine structure as solved by Pelletier and Caventou in 1820. Their 1820 paper, S4, establishes the chemical investigation, separation and naming used here, not the full structure; no structure-discovery date is assigned in this record.
gaps: The initial observer, the precise first medicinal indication, whether the earliest observation was planned or accidental, and the chain from Indigenous knowledge to later antimalarial use remain unresolved.
The seventeenth-century accounts of bark use were read through historical reviews, not in their original editions; no contemporary first-person Jesuit account of the initial transfer was located.

Only the specified relevant pages of the 1820 chemical and 1823 clinical reports were read; the original sources for all later treatment and derivative-priority claims were not exhaustively investigated.

classes.name: Non-ergot dopamine receptor agonists

starting.description: Known dopamine-receptor agonist effects of ergot/ergoline drugs stimulated the developers to examine simpler indolone compounds. An active 7-hydroxy indolone with dopamine-like cardiovascular effects was prior art and was used as starting material in one route to the des-hydroxy compound. Separately, apomorphine's observed animal motor effects informed early Parkinson's research.

inspiration.description: Observed effects of known ergot/ergoline-derived dopamine agonists motivated the indolone program, while dopamine's cardiovascular activity and that of a dopamine-mimicking 7-hydroxy indolone supplied physiological and pharmacological reference points. An independent apomorphine branch followed observed animal motor effects. Ergot agents are historical inspirations, not members of the assigned class.

steps.description: Researchers observed dopamine-receptor agonism among existing ergot/ergoline compounds and used those working effects as a starting clue for a simpler peripheral D2 agonist.
The 7-hydroxy indolone series showed reported dopamine-like cardiovascular effects; its di-n-propyl congener was developed as an active predecessor.

Chemists prepared and tested des-hydroxy indolones, including the compound later called ropinirole; the inventor used the active 7-hydroxy congener in one route and reported retained D2 and cardiovascular effects.

The same indolone compound was subsequently investigated for Parkinson's disease, as documented by an early small open clinical study; the reason and timing of the therapeutic shift are not established here.

In a separate earlier branch, apomorphine's observed effects on animal movement helped motivate clinical investigation in Parkinson's disease; the 1951 clinical observations predated the later dopamine-receptor explanation.

design.description: The team hypothesized an active ergoline fragment, designed and tested simpler indolones without the full ergot or catechol framework, and prepared a des-hydroxy compound with reported D2 activity. The work created and evaluated a changed molecular architecture for a selective pharmacological goal, not merely a delivery formulation.

circumstances.description: The named event is the deliberate synthesis and pharmacological testing of indolones as selective peripheral D2 agonists; this does not assert that every result was expected or that the earlier biological clues were planned.

classes.name: Neprilysin inhibitors

starting.description: For the early neuronal line, observations of enkephalin degradation and enzyme localization led Roques and colleagues to test whether inhibition would protect endogenous opioid signalling. Separately, atrial extracts produced natriuresis, and ANP was observed to be degraded by endopeptidase 24.11 in vitro; Ksander's cardiovascular patent explicitly proposed inhibiting that enzyme to prolong ANF's biological actions. The 1995 paper also records earlier NEP-inhibitor clinical experience as motivation for improved compounds. These lines share enzyme biology, but a direct thiorphan-to-sacubitril chemical lineage is not established.

inspiration.description: Enkephalins and their observed cleavage informed the neuronal question; the natriuretic effects of atrial extracts and NEP-mediated cleavage of endogenous ANP/ANF informed the cardiovascular strategy. The 1995 authors also cite prior inhibitor effects and modest clinical outcomes when explaining their search for improved pharmacology. This does not assert that an earlier synthetic candidate was the direct chemical parent of sacubitril.

steps.description: In the neuronal line, Roques and colleagues deliberately designed thiorphan to investigate an observed enkephalin-cleaving enzyme and a hypothesized role in opioid signalling; their abstract reports enkephalin protection and naloxone-sensitive antinociception.
In a separate physiological line, de Bold and colleagues observed marked natriuresis and diuresis after administering atrial tissue extracts to rats, with ventricular extract and medium controls.
Stephenson and Kenny observed hydrolysis of human ANP in pig kidney preparations in vitro and inhibition of the products by phosphoramidon; the 1995 inhibitor paper later cited their study.

Ksander's patent proposed protecting the natriuretic, diuretic and vascular actions of ANF by inhibiting its enzymatic degradation, and disclosed synthetic biaryl aminobutyric-acid amide esters and acids.

Ksander and colleagues synthesized and tested new inhibitor series. The 1995 original calls 19a the ethyl ester prodrug of active acid 21a, compares stereoisomers, and reports animal tests involving administered ANF; its authors did not claim those tests proved enhanced endogenous ANF.

The 1995 ester/acid and stereoisomer data align with the later identification of sacubitril as the ester prodrug of LBQ657 and Schiering's attribution of LBQ657 stereoisomers to that study, supporting an inferred mapping of 19a to sacubitril and 21a to LBQ657. Braunwald retrospectively describes the 1995 report as sacubitril; the 1995 passages inspected do not use the later names.
The 2016 structure visualizes LBQ657 bound to NEP and provides later mechanistic interpretation of its interactions; it does not establish the method used to create the original inhibitor.

design.description: The neuronal team used enzyme-specificity and metallopeptidase reasoning in designing a synthetic thiol-containing inhibitor. The cardiovascular inventors deliberately synthesized new biaryl amino-butyric-acid amides, varied side chains and stereochemistry, compared inhibitory activity and pharmacological properties, and prepared an ethyl ester prodrug and active acid. These are substantive chemical invention and optimization, not merely extracting a natural molecule or adjusting delivery. Their existence does not erase the biological observations motivating the programs; thiorphan's direct chemical parentage of sacubitril is not established.

circumstances.description: The specified events were deliberate design of thiorphan to investigate enkephalinase and a planned cardiovascular program to inhibit ANF-degrading NEP, followed by systematic synthesis and testing. This is not a claim that every earlier physiological observation or later finding was expected.

classes.name: Anthraquinone stimulant laxatives

starting.description: The purgative effect of senna leaves and fruits was recognized in medicinal use, and preparations were developed from the plant; the first observer and initial circumstances are not established.

inspiration.description: Observed purgative activity of senna plant material in medicinal use; the original individual observation is not described.

steps.description: A modern historical account connects recognition of senna's purgative action with the use of its powders and preparations. By 1949 senna leaf and pod were established vegetable purgatives.

Fairbairn reports earlier crystallization of sennosides A and B and investigates active constituents of already used plant purgatives; the 1949 Stoll and colleagues abstract describes their isolation and purification method.

Later researchers compare variable liquid senna preparations with a dry granular senna-pod preparation using chemical, animal, and clinical assessments; they report stability and activity for the tested dry preparation.

design.description: Researchers isolated and crystallized natural senna glycosides, compared their biological activity with chemically treated fractions, developed chemical and biological assays, and evaluated a dry granular preparation to address consistency and stability of the established plant drug. The sources do not establish a newly designed active molecule or identify who invented the granular formulation.

circumstances.description: Fairbairn's comparison of purified and chemically altered sennoside A was a planned experiment; the circumstances of the original observation remain unknown.

classes.name: PDE5 inhibitors

starting.description: Known nitrate-responsive vascular relaxation and prior atrial natriuretic peptide work informed a proposed cardiovascular strategy of preserving cGMP. Pfizer developed the already active weak PDE inhibitor zaprinast into potent, selective compounds. In a separate Glaxo branch, an empirically PDE5-active screening hit, GR30040x, was selected for further development; the reason it entered that screen remains disputed.

inspiration.description: The Pfizer cardiovascular rationale drew on nitrate-responsive vascular biology, the benefits and limitations of nitrate treatment, and prior atrial natriuretic peptide work; its chemical starting point was the already active synthetic inhibitor zaprinast. In the Glaxo branch, a measured PDE5-active compound was selected for development, while the functional role of reported β-carboline effects in selecting it is contested. These are distinct biological, clinical and chemical contributions.

steps.description: The Pfizer cardiovascular project considered preserving cGMP by targeting PDE5 in light of nitrate action, tolerance and prior atrial natriuretic peptide research.

Starting with the already active inhibitor zaprinast, the team used modelling and medicinal-chemistry optimization to improve potency, PDE5 selectivity and pharmacokinetic properties, leading to sildenafil.
Subsequent volunteer-reported erections and physiological data helped motivate ED pilot studies.
In a separate Glaxo cardiovascular project, measured PDE5 inhibition led to selection of GR30040x for further research. The upstream cause of its inclusion in the screen is contested.

The tadalafil team's medicinal chemistry modified a PDE5-active hydantoin lead into a piperazinedione series and optimized substitution and stereochemistry, producing a cardiovascular development candidate later used for ED.

design.description: Researchers intentionally selected PDE5 and used modelling and medicinal chemistry to develop the existing weak zaprinast activity into a potent, selective pyrazolopyrimidinone series, optimizing pharmacokinetics as well. In the separate Glaxo branch, substantial ring-architecture changes from a PDE5-active hydantoin to a piperazinedione, with substitution and stereochemical optimization, produced tadalafil.

circumstances.description: The cardiovascular pathway approach was proposed intentionally; the later volunteer reports were side effects rather than the initial program target.

classes.name: Fluoride anticaries preparations

starting.description: Long before the Colorado findings, an 1874 preventive proposal drew on a reported animal-enamel observation, and an 1892 address linked fluoride in enamel and diet to a hypothesis about decay. Their connection to the later sodium-fluoride program is unestablished. In the directly documented 20th-century topical lineage, unexpectedly low apparent decay in mottled teeth, fluoride in associated natural waters, and observations in enamel and animals motivated controlled preventive fluoride applications.

inspiration.description: Naturally occurring fluoride in domestic water and observed relationships with caries and enamel, complemented by enamel uptake and animal observations, motivated controlled fluoride exposure in the documented 20th-century lineage. Earlier fluoride-enamel observations and an animal effect were reported alongside separate 19th-century preventive ideas.

steps.description: Before the Colorado work, Erhardt's 1874 preventive recommendation was linked by a later historian to a reported animal-enamel effect, and Crichton-Browne's 1892 address connected enamel fluoride and dietary change to a caries hypothesis. Their continuity to the later topical program is not established.
McKay and Black noted mottling alongside unexpectedly low apparent decay, and the waterborne fluoride explanation was identified later.

Dean compared population exposure and caries, then proposed controlled fluoride use in drinking water; topical researchers later explicitly cited his epidemiology alongside enamel and animal experiments.

Earlier topical work with sodium or potassium fluoride was reported in 1942; Knutson and Armstrong subsequently tested topical sodium fluoride against untreated teeth and a separate untreated group, reporting less new caries after one year.

design.description: Researchers translated observational clues into hypotheses for controlled water exposure and selected and tested a topical sodium-fluoride solution. This was adaptation of fluoride delivery and treatment procedure, not evidence of inventing a new active structure; the authors did not establish an optimum concentration.

circumstances.description: The apparent resistance of mottled teeth was unexpected in the retrospective account; the later controlled-exposure hypotheses and topical trial were deliberate.

Neither the origin of every oral or topical vehicle nor priority of every fluoride preparation is established; later water fluoridation should not be presented as a prerequisite for the already reported 1942–43 topical studies.
conflicts: A historical review attributes stronger dog enamel to Erhardt's 1874 potassium-fluoride work, but also reports Stubenrauch's 1904 observations of dental and skeletal damage after sodium fluoride. Different conditions are not established and neither original report was read; the claims cannot be directly reconciled here.
gaps: Erhardt's 1874 original article or articles and Stubenrauch's 1904 original were not read; exact methods and continuity to later sodium-fluoride work remain uncertain.
The 1892 Lancet address was read only through a selective 2004 reprint; earlier proposed uses cannot be assigned priority from it.
The 1916 Black–McKay and 1942 Bibby/Cheyne originals and the origins of all later fluoride vehicles were not independently read; accounts are attributed to the sources actually examined.

classes.name: Antibacterial sulfonamides

starting.description: A planned search for antistreptococcal agents yielded the observation that Prontosil, a synthetic sulfonamide-containing azo dye, protected experimentally infected animals. Domagk's 1935 indexed abstract reports mouse survival after treatment; Bickel's history says its publication prompted the Pasteur group's investigations of related compounds. The antibacterial intention preceded the result, but the observed in-vivo effect supplied a working lead for subsequent development.

inspiration.description: The relevant observations were protection of infected animals by the synthetic dye Prontosil and subsequent therapeutic activity of the colorless compound sulfanilamide. Under Ha's broad definition, observing and developing these biological effects counts as nature-inspired biological inspiration; it does not imply that the molecules or their scaffold were isolated from nature.

steps.description: Bickel describes a planned antistreptococcal screen of dyes and heavy-metal compounds. The reported protective effect of Prontosil in infected mice was an observed result of that search, not the same event as deciding to screen; Domagk's indexed 1935 abstract also reports survival of treated infected mice.

Bickel says Domagk's publication prompted the Pasteur group's work on related compounds. The reproduced opening and closing fragments of their 1935 report connect that work with the therapeutic activity of a simple colorless non-dye compound; Domagk retrospectively credits the group with the first publication of sulfanilamide's therapeutic activity.

Bickel, citing Bovet, says the Pasteur group proposed metabolic cleavage after demonstrating sulfanilamide activity. He attributes later analytical identification of conjugated sulfanilamide in urine from Prontosil-treated patients and mice to Fuller in 1937; that analytical original was not read here. The 1935 proposal and the later analytical evidence are distinct.

Gray, Buttle and Stephenson explicitly state in 1937 that the prior sulfanilamide mouse-protection finding led them to investigate related compounds. They report qualifications on measured differences and toxicity, so their study is evidence of derivative research, not universal superiority.

Further chemistry included heterocyclic substitution and compounds with different antibacterial properties, as Domagk retrospectively describes. Such changes could affect activity or spectrum and are not necessarily mere formulation or delivery optimization.

Bickel places the Woods and Fildes account of antagonism involving para-aminobenzoic acid in 1940, after the founding observations and early derivative work. The later mechanism should not be presented as the original design rationale.

design.description: Researchers planned and performed biological screens, investigated dye-related structures and the simpler active sulfanilamide, and made and compared later derivatives, including heterocyclic substitutions. These are deliberate experimental and chemical contributions following or testing observed activity; structural changes can alter antibacterial properties and are not confined to delivery. The sources here do not establish the particular design route of sulfamethoxazole.

circumstances.description: This value is scoped to the founding antistreptococcal screening program described by Bickel, not to every later experiment. For the separate Pasteur sulfanilamide test, Bickel attributes a deliberate primary aim to Bovet, whereas Christensen describes an accidental test and surprise; the available fragments do not resolve that disagreement. A surprising result can coexist with a planned test, but that possibility does not resolve why this test was performed.

Their primary reports were not read here; the discrepancy does not erase the documented observation that prompted development.
gaps: The full 1935 Domagk article, the experimental middle and full text of the 1935 Pasteur report, the underlying Bovet personal communication and relevant contemporary laboratory records were not read; these gaps limit reconstruction of the test's motivation and priority.

classes.name: Triptans

starting.description: Clinical observations that intravenous serotonin could relieve migraine, despite substantial adverse effects, motivated a search for the receptor responsible for its beneficial action and a more selective agonist. Clinical and animal observations involving methysergide also helped focus the team's receptor hypothesis.

inspiration.description: The starting clues included a reported clinical effect of the endogenous signaling molecule serotonin, clinical responses to methysergide, and methysergide's observed action in an animal carotid circulation. Researchers sought to separate beneficial from unwanted serotonin effects through receptor selectivity.

steps.description: Reports of migraine relief following intravenous serotonin, tempered by problematic side effects, gave the Glaxo team a clinical effect to develop.
Lance's clinical observations and Saxena's animal work on methysergide, followed by the team's own experiments, focused attention on a potentially distinct serotonin receptor in cranial circulation.
The team sought the relevant serotonin receptor and designed selective agonists; the research led to sumatriptan.
An early open clinical study reported responses to intravenous GR43175; Humphrey later attributed the development of similar triptans to sumatriptan's clinical success.

design.description: Deliberate design created a serotonin-related molecule with a different receptor-selectivity profile, aiming to retain the desired effect while reducing other serotonin effects.

circumstances.description: The Glaxo team's receptor search and development of selective agonists were deliberate; this does not characterize the circumstances of the earlier clinical observation.

classes.name: Androgens

starting.description: Castration and testicular transplantation revealed a relationship between testicular tissue and male secondary characteristics. Later, bioactive testis extracts and comparisons with urinary androsterone supplied observable activities and chemical constraints in the search for the active testicular hormone. The evidence does not establish a direct line of personal influence from Berthold's particular experiment to each 1930s investigator.

inspiration.description: The effects of loss or transplantation of testicular tissue, active extracts, and the endogenous hormone eventually identified as testosterone. Synthesis responded to observed biological and chemical clues.

steps.description: Castration and transplantation experiments established a testicular influence on secondary sexual characteristics and suggested an action via the blood.
Popular but unsubstantiated organotherapy helped motivate competition to isolate the testicular hormone; comparative tests also distinguished urinary androsterone from testicular activity.

Comparative testis-extract and urinary-androsterone observations informed structural hypotheses and preparation of candidates from cholesterol; at approximately the same time the testicular hormone was isolated and matched a synthetic candidate.

A 1939 clinical case report describes testosterone in oil and then testosterone propionate administered for suspected deficiency beginning in 1936. It demonstrates early clinical application, not first use or controlled efficacy.

design.description: Růžička's group reasoned from physiological and chemical findings to structural candidates, then prepared candidates from cholesterol; one matched the hormone isolated from testes.

circumstances.description: Berthold deliberately performed the removal and transplantation experiment; its initial hypothesis is not stated in the translated report. Růžička's group later deliberately proposed and synthesized structural candidates. This is not a claim about whether every earlier finding was expected.

classes.name: Vitamin B1 preparations

starting.description: An unexpected beriberi-like chicken outbreak coincided with feeding polished rice and abated when that feeding arrangement ended. Eijkman reports planned comparative feeding experiments showing disease on polished rice and protection with unpolished rice, leading researchers toward the protective material in rice's outer portions; Grijns later interpreted the problem as loss of a needed dietary substance.

inspiration.description: The operative clue was the animal disease–diet relationship, followed by protective activity in rice outer layers and other foods and extracts. Those biological observations guided isolation of the factor later identified as thiamine; the category does not depend on the current method of manufacture.

steps.description: An unexpected laboratory chicken outbreak, followed by deliberate polished-versus-unpolished-rice feeding experiments, pointed to a diet-related protective factor in the outer portions of rice.
Grijns advanced a deficiency interpretation; Eijkman describes protective foods and concentrated extracts and their application to bird polyneuritis and human beriberi.

Jansen and Donath reported crystalline anti-beriberi material from rice polishings in 1926; subsequent animal testing found antineuritic activity, while a 1930 replication team could not establish the crystals' purity.

After work on the vitamin's structure, Cline, Williams, and Finkelstein described chemical synthesis and physiological comparison with the naturally obtained vitamin; an institutional history recounts later commercial thiamine production for nutritional use.

design.description: Researchers designed comparative animal-feeding experiments, extracted and fractionated protective material using biological activity as a guide, investigated the vitamin's structure, and developed a chemical synthesis that reproduced the known vitamin. Industrial production then made thiamine available for nutritional use. This is a designed manufacturing route to an observed nutrient, not evidence of a de novo therapeutic concept.

circumstances.description: Eijkman's laboratory outbreak and the food change that exposed the association were unexpected; the subsequent comparative feeding experiments and later chemical synthesis were planned investigations.

Synthesis priority among contemporaneous groups and the complete primary history of clinical formulations and commercial production were not investigated; the class-level judgment does not require resolving those questions.

classes.name: Dual GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonists

starting.description: Greater weight and fat reduction from co-administered GIP and GLP-1 analogues in obese mice supplied Finan's team with an experimental reason to pursue a single dual agonist. The LY3298176 investigators cited this prior combination result among the biological reasons for pursuing GIP addition to GLP-1 activity.

inspiration.description: The observed combined actions of GIP and GLP-1 analogues, along with incretin physiology and the hormone-derived peptide sequences, informed the engineering. The LY3298176 authors specifically cite the Finan combination findings and call their peptide GIP-based; a later investigator account describes adding GLP-1 activity to a GIP sequence.

steps.description: Combining selective incretin analogues enhanced weight-lowering in diet-induced obese mice relative to either alone at the tested doses, leading the investigators to pursue a single co-agonist.
Investigators built and tested a sequence-modified peptide with GIP and GLP-1 activity from a previously studied dual GLP-1/glucagon peptide, then modified candidates to extend exposure.

Citing prior dual incretin studies including the co-administration experiment, Lilly investigators developed a GIP-based, fatty-acid-modified dual agonist, LY3298176, and tested both receptor activities in cells and mice. They later identified LY3298176 as tirzepatide and described engineering GLP-1 activity into the GIP sequence.
The LY3298176 investigators reported a phase 1 clinical program and a four-week proof-of-concept trial in type 2 diabetes.

design.description: The Finan team engineered balanced receptor co-agonism and selectivity by sequence changes and lengthened exposure by lipidation or PEGylation. LY3298176, or tirzepatide, is a different GIP-based engineered peptide, with GLP-1 activity introduced into the GIP sequence, stronger GIPR than GLP-1R potency in the reported in-vitro assays and a fatty-acid linker to enable prolonged exposure.

circumstances.description: The comparison of co-administered analogues and subsequent single-peptide engineering were planned experiments in the Finan program; the Lilly team designed LY3298176 to test dual incretin activity.

sources.citation: Finan B, Ma T, Ottaway N, et al. 2013. Unimolecular dual incretins maximize metabolic benefits in rodents, monkeys, and humans. Sci Transl Med 5(209):209ra151. DOI 10.1126/scitranslmed.3007218; PMID 24174327.

classes.name: Sulfamate-substituted monosaccharide anticonvulsants

starting.description: A synthetic sugar-derived intermediate, selected for planned mouse seizure testing because of its structure, showed anticonvulsant activity. The observed effect supplied the starting point for developing it for epilepsy.

inspiration.description: Anticonvulsant effect observed in a mouse electroshock assay of a pre-existing synthetic sugar-derived intermediate. The earlier program sought analogues of fructose-1,6-diphosphate for a metabolic-enzyme objective; this chemical context is distinct from the observed seizure effect.

steps.description: The compound was made as an intermediate in a program seeking metabolic-enzyme inhibitors for a potential antidiabetic treatment, then selected for a targeted anticonvulsant assay on the basis of structure.
Its observed mouse anticonvulsant effect prompted further evaluation and eventual preclinical development; a contemporaneous patent disclosed both the synthetic compound and animal seizure-test data.
The 1987 report identified the active sugar sulfamate as topiramate and described synthesis and anticonvulsant testing of related analogues.
The candidate progressed through clinical development and received FDA approval for epilepsy in late 1996.

design.description: Researchers made the sulfamate derivative of protected fructose, selected it for seizure testing using a structural clue, assembled supporting pharmacology, pursued preclinical development and synthesized and tested related analogues. The accessible 1987 abstract does not establish that any particular later analogue became a marketed medicine.

circumstances.description: Gardocki deliberately selected the compound for mouse anticonvulsant testing. The cited account does not establish whether the positive result itself was unexpected.

classes.name: Serotonin antagonist and reuptake inhibitors

starting.description: Developers described an observed clinical picture of depression including mental pain, which prompted the hypothesis that raising the threshold for unpleasant experience could have antidepressant effects. They used animal models accordingly and later described antinociception as critical to trazodone's discovery.

inspiration.description: A clinical observation of mental pain among depressed patients led to the hypothesis about threshold for unpleasant experiences, as reconstructed retrospectively by the developer; its validity as a disease mechanism is a separate question.

steps.description: Retrospective developer accounts connect the observed mental-pain clinical picture to a hypothesis about unpleasant experiences and hypothesis-directed animal models.

Researchers synthesized a triazolopyridinone and reported pain-related, behavioral and peripheral antiserotonin assays. A developer later described antinociception as critical to discovery; Ban recounts subsequent clinical investigations.
Later characterization described serotonin reuptake inhibition and high 5-HT2 affinity for trazodone.

A later related phenoxyethyl-triazolone development combined new chemistry with receptor-binding selection. The 1982 patent's preferred compound was subsequently identified as nefazodone; company researchers describe initial 5-HT2A blocking and reduced alpha-1 potency followed by in-vitro uptake characterization.

design.description: Researchers translated a clinical idea into animal tests and synthesized the trazodone triazolopyridinone; the patent does not state why that structure was first selected. A later phenoxyethyl-triazolone series, including nefazodone, used a different architecture and serotonin/alpha-receptor binding profile in the search for antidepressants with fewer side effects. That is later medicinal chemistry and pharmacology, not evidence that the original class was designed from scratch.

circumstances.description: The use of animal models to pursue the mental-pain hypothesis was purposeful; this does not establish whether discovering the particular compound or any other effect was expected.

The complete 1984 and 1989 Silvestrini papers were not accessible; only their abstracts were read. The 1985 chapter's complete Introduction and first two pages were read, not the full five-page chapter.

The full 1995 Taylor et al. review and original internal nefazodone discovery records were not read; the documented receptor-focused branch rests on its abstract and the 1982 and 1986 patent passages.

classes.name: Antibacterial dihydrofolate-reductase inhibitors

starting.description: Known bacterial nutrient-growth requirements motivated the L. casei assay and studies of thymine-related bases. Synthetic base analogues then inhibited this model and pathogens; the team developed a diaminopyrimidine series and studied folate-dependent growth responses.

inspiration.description: Known nutrient-dependent bacterial growth informed the assay, with the natural nucleic-acid base thymine a reference for studying related structures; inhibition by synthetic base analogues and differential responses to folate forms informed subsequent development.

steps.description: Known folate, thymine and purine relationships in bacterial growth motivated the L. casei model and studies of thymine analogues; synthetic analogues inhibited that system and pathogenic bacteria.

Falco began a diaminopyrimidine series; the team observed folate-antagonist activity in L. casei and differential folic-versus-folinic-acid growth responses that supported a folate-reduction interpretation.

For antibacterial use, the team selected among 5-benzylpyrimidines for selectivity and other useful properties. They reported trimethoprim's stronger antibacterial action than earlier candidates and the absence of their particular side effects in monkeys.

In a 1965 enzyme study the group reported distinct species-specific inhibition patterns and a correlation between drug binding and suppression of the source organism. The available abstract does not identify which compounds were tested.
The group tested trimethoprim with sulfonamides in bacterial cultures and mouse infections, reporting potentiation in selected settings.

design.description: The group synthesized and screened base analogues, developed and selected 2,4-diaminopyrimidines with differential antimicrobial activity, selected trimethoprim for antibacterial properties and tolerability in the stated tests, and investigated sulfonamide combinations.

circumstances.description: The initial synthetic-analogue investigation and use of observed biological differences were deliberate. According to the 1993 review's abstract, substituted diaminopyrimidines' interference with folate utilization rather than the expected thymine antagonism was unexpected; the underlying original account for that expectation was not read.

classes.name: Acyclic guanosine-analogue antivirals

starting.description: Antiviral activity of purine analogues anchored the existing program. Elion and Vince recount that Schaeffer's acyclic adenine analogue was observed to be an adenosine-deaminase substrate, suggesting recognition by other enzymes; its observed antiherpes activity led to development of acyclic antivirals. Other accounts describe a different initial inhibitor intention; see conflicts.

inspiration.description: The precursor chemistry modified adenosine, the enzyme's normal substrate; observed enzyme recognition of an acyclic analogue and antiviral activity of related synthetic compounds supplied the aciclovir program's clues.

steps.description: Existing antiviral findings motivated a purine-arabinoside research program, in which diaminopurine arabinoside had measurable antiviral activity.

A substrate observation on an acyclic adenine analogue suggested other enzymes might recognize the non-ring side chain, and an antiviral screen then revealed antiherpes activity and redirected the program toward acyclic analogues.
The guanine analogue aciclovir was unexpectedly much more active than the corresponding diaminopurine analogue.

The existing antiviral aciclovir was adapted into amino-acid esters. A later deliberate oral-prodrug program compared them in rats and selected the L-valyl ester, 256U87, which became valaciclovir; its absorption advantage was not predicted by the first solubility observations.

design.description: Researchers intentionally designed modified adenosine sugar analogues, synthesized and screened purine arabinosides and acyclic nucleoside analogues, compared base substitutions, and investigated selectivity. Later amino-acid esterification of existing aciclovir and comparative animal testing yielded the L-valine prodrug valaciclovir.

circumstances.description: Acyclic analogues were deliberately synthesized and tested, whereas the much greater activity of the guanine analogue was unexpected. Vince describes hypothesis-directed submission of the adenine precursor for antiviral testing, while Biron calls the aciclovir screen random. The later oral-prodrug comparison was planned; the earlier ester group's initial solubility observations did not predict its oral-absorption advantage.

classes.name: Fatty-acid / valproate anticonvulsants

starting.description: In the account attributed to the investigators, two dissimilar experimental solutions shared the same solvent and protected against induced seizures; the team inferred that dipropylacetic acid might itself be anticonvulsant. A later review instead alleges reduced seizures in patients given valproate-containing cough syrup, while another account invokes physical similarity to phenytoin; the precise first observation remains contested.

inspiration.description: The detailed laboratory account attributes the clue to seizure protection associated with pre-existing synthetic solvent dipropylacetic acid, inferred from unrelated solutions sharing the vehicle. A conflicting later review alleges a patient effect instead; this clinical clue is reported, not independently established.

steps.description: A khellin-derived test solution and a chemically different coumarin solution, both dissolved in dipropylacetic acid, showed seizure protection, leading researchers to suspect the solvent.
According to Monneret, the acid was converted to sodium valproate for clinical use; initial clinical results were published in 1964 and marketing authorization followed in 1967.

A 1967 patent reported separate animal tests of the acid and sodium salt against induced seizures, showing testing beyond the original mixed solutions without establishing the date or priority of those examples.

A 1974 original clinical series reported sodium-valproate use in patients with epilepsy, illustrating later uptake; treatment changes and absence of a described randomized control limit interpretation.

design.description: Researchers prepared and pharmacologically tested solutes, compared seizure protection across unrelated solutions and inferred the common solvent's possible role; subsequent clinical development used the sodium salt.

circumstances.description: The researchers deliberately tested the solutions, including against cardiazol-induced seizures; identifying their shared solvent as the likely source of protection was an unexpected finding.

classes.name: Phenylalkylamine calcium-channel blockers

starting.description: Papaverine's known smooth-muscle-relaxing and antispasmodic effects, including its use for intestinal colic, supplied a working natural-product lead for the synthetic D365/verapamil line, as reported retrospectively by Davies and Hollman.

inspiration.description: The molecular-development starting point was papaverine, an opium alkaloid with known smooth-muscle-relaxing and intestinal antispasmodic effects. Subsequently, observed cardiac effects of already synthesized verapamil and prenylamine led to recognition of calcium antagonism; that later mechanistic clue did not precede synthesis of the drugs.

steps.description: Papaverine's observed smooth-muscle relaxation and intestinal antispasmodic use preceded and, according to Davies and Hollman, led to the D365 analogue line.
Dengel's invention specified a synthetic phenylacetonitrile series for coronary vasodilatation and reported D365's experimental activity relative to papaverine.
The later history reports that the D365 compound was developed as verapamil, entered angina trials in 1961, and was marketed as Isoptin.

Fleckenstein investigated unexpected cardiac depression with the already synthesized coronary drugs verapamil and prenylamine. Their similarity to calcium withdrawal and reversibility with calcium helped establish the calcium-antagonist concept, named in 1969.

design.description: Researchers synthesized a novel phenylacetonitrile series and studied its coronary-dilating activity; the historical accounts call D365 a synthetic analogue of papaverine, a benzylisoquinoline. This is an appreciable architectural change, but the sources read do not specify the complete sequence by which it was achieved.

circumstances.description: The patent-stage search for coronary vasodilatation was planned; Fleckenstein described the later recognition of calcium antagonism while investigating unexpected cardiac depression as a chance discovery.

limits: The papaverine-to-verapamil classification concerns the assigned verapamil line, not separate dihydropyridine or benzothiazepine families.

Prenylamine contributed a distinct co-observation to the calcium-antagonist concept, but the sources read do not establish that it followed the papaverine-to-verapamil chemical-development pathway; the judgment is not an origin classification of prenylamine's separate molecular line.
conflicts: Davies and Hollman 2002 (E1) date the D365 analogue to 1957; Hollman 1991 (E5) says May 1959. The sources share an author and the discrepancy remains unresolved.
gaps: The original Dengel/Knoll notebook or project rationale has not been read; the specific papaverine-to-D365 causal attribution rests on retrospective accounts rather than the patent's pharmacological comparator alone.
Fleckenstein's 1983 original review was read only as an abstract, with an additional passage reproduced by a later review; the contemporaneous 1964 experimental report has not been read.
The 1962 Haas-Haertfelder original pharmacology article was located as metadata without an abstract and was not read.
The intermediate chemical-development sequence and the precise date of first D365 synthesis are not resolved by the materials read.

classes.name: Vitamin K antagonists

starting.description: Veterinary investigation linked a serious cattle bleeding and clotting disorder to spoiled sweet-clover hay. Link's laboratory developed the observed biological effect into an assay-guided search for the hay's active hemorrhagic factor, leading to crystalline dicumarol. Link later reported a farmer's visit as a further stimulus, but Burris questioned details of that retrospective anecdote; the founding observation does not depend on it.

inspiration.description: The inspiration was the observed hemorrhagic and impaired-coagulation effect in livestock fed spoiled sweet-clover hay, followed through bioassay to dicumarol isolated from that material. The later drug warfarin was a synthetic analogue, not a compound shown here to have been isolated from hay.

steps.description: Veterinarians linked cattle hemorrhage and impaired coagulation with spoiled sweet-clover hay; the laboratory took up the agricultural problem. Link later reported a chance 1933 farmer encounter as an additional stimulus, with details expressly questioned by Burris.

Bioassay-guided extraction led to a crystalline hemorrhagic factor, and structural work identified it as dicumarol; synthesis produced material matching the isolated product chemically and in animal effects.
By 1940, the laboratory was deliberately preparing related compounds and considering their potential medical use, seeking synthetic analogues with stronger effects than the identified lead.

Rat work published in 1942 documented that vitamin K counteracted dicumarol-induced hypoprothrombinemia, a physiological relationship relevant to the class, without resolving its molecular mechanism in that paper.
The laboratory prepared and assayed further related 4-hydroxycoumarin structures; no. 42 was selected after animal testing and developed as warfarin.
Warfarin was marketed for rodent control and later used clinically in a more water-soluble sodium form; ACS dates human-use approval to 1954.

design.description: Researchers synthesized the identified active hay compound, made structurally related 4-hydroxycoumarin analogues, compared their biological effects across animal models, selected warfarin no. 42, and developed a more water-soluble sodium form. The analogue series changes active structure and biological activity; it is not merely a delivery adjustment. These intentional contributions follow the observed hemorrhagic lead.

circumstances.description: The designation combines an observed livestock disease and Link's reported chance farmer visit with deliberate assay-guided isolation, synthesis and analogue development. Details of the retrospective visit are questioned by Burris; the chance encounter is a reported circumstance, not an independently established scene or a necessary premise of the observation-led judgment.

limits: The supported founding chain is the assigned spoiled-hay–dicumarol–warfarin 4-hydroxycoumarin lineage. The cohort member is warfarin; other vitamin K antagonist founding lineages were not investigated and should not be inferred from this record.

Dicumarol was identified in spoiled hay, but warfarin no. 42 was a later synthetic analogue. Compound no. 63 was a distinct related compound, not warfarin; it is not treated as a separate founding branch here.
The 1942 vitamin K study establishes an experimental physiological antagonism in rats; no modern molecular mechanism or causally necessary design rationale is inferred from it.
conflicts: Burris1994 p.183 explicitly questions details of Link's1959 farmer-visit narrative, citing late-recorded quotations, changes in reported journey and weather, discrepancies with original documents and recollections of early workers. The visit is retained as Link's report with this uncertainty; the livestock observations and laboratory development do not depend on its dramatic details.

Link's 1959 retrospective reports that early clinical reports denied vitamin K reversal of dicumarol's action, whereas the 1942 Overman animal experiment reports antagonism. Species and contexts differ; these sources do not by themselves adjudicate every early clinical observation.

A non-founding anecdote differs: Burris says Eisenhower received dicumarol after his heart attack, while ACS says warfarin. The treatment detail was not independently adjudicated and is not used in the origin judgment.
gaps: Final source review independently read indexed OCR with the correct 1941 title, authors and pages for Stahmann, Huebner and Link. The live PDF route redirected to a different 1944 article and the publisher PDF was blocked. The indexed 1941 text supports the stated structure/synthesis and rabbit prothrombin comparisons; it does not provide a complete multispecies dose-response report or replace the separate original isolation paper. Downloadable 1941 PDF/page images remained unavailable.
The contemporaneous original veterinary publications of Schofield and Roderick were not separately read; their observations are attributed to Link's retrospective.

The separate Campbell and Link isolation report, the 1903 chemical synthesis report cited in the reproduced letter, and Link's original 1940 letter were not separately read. The 1941 structure/synthesis paper and the text of the letter reproduced by Burris were read.
The early warfarin clinical papers and primary approval records were not separately read; establishment and the 1954 approval year are attributed to the Link and ACS retrospective accounts.

The original 1941 and 1942 papers were read through indexed or hosted full-text transcriptions; downloadable PDFs were not obtained. The ACS source was read in a web index. Source access does not establish independent verification of every passage.

classes.name: Z-drug hypnotics
classes.scopeNote: Basis scope: zolpidem; zopiclone's initial screening purpose unresolved.

starting.description: Documented support is bounded to Kaplan's zolpidem branch: he recalls a 1978 request for a zopiclone-like compound and a structural-hybrid proposal based on the drugs' similar actions. Wermuth's 2006 profile-directed zopiclone account conflicts with his 2008 extensive/random-screening framing; the initiating zopiclone purpose remains unresolved.

inspiration.description: For the documented zolpidem branch, known synthetic-drug actions and Kaplan's proposed shared-receptor relationship motivated hybrid design. The initial zopiclone screening purpose remains disputed. This is broad biological inspiration, without a claim of natural-molecule ancestry or an established initiating clue for zopiclone.

steps.description: According to Wermuth's 2006 retrospective, after benzodiazepine anxiolytic and tranquilizing effects became known, Rhône-Poulenc searched for functionally similar compounds and obtained zopiclone. His 2008 screening classification leaves the exact initial screening objective and stages uncertain; neither account establishes the earliest assay sequence or chemical starting structure.

A 1972-priority patent disclosed the pyrrolopyrazine series and the structure assigned to zopiclone; it reported behavioral pharmacology for the series. The 1983 zopiclone study abstract later reported benzodiazepine-like pharmacological activity.
Kaplan recalls a 1978 request for a zopiclone-like compound, followed by physical comparison of drug models and a deliberate hybrid-design proposal written with George.

Kaplan and George patented an imidazopyridine series with 1980 priority; Kaplan identifies its compound 75 as zolpidem. A 1985 original-study abstract reports receptor binding and rat electrocorticographic effects of zolpidem.

design.description: Researchers synthesized and tested a distinct pyrrolopyrazine series; Wermuth's accounts differ in how the initial screening objective is framed. For the later branch, Kaplan reports comparing physical structures and proposing hybrids; the team pursued substituted imidazopyridines, including compound 75. The sources do not establish an exact discovery-stage optimization pathway or justify attributing all series-level patent test outcomes to either named compound.

circumstances.description: The particular planned stage was Kaplan's reported structural-hybrid project following the zopiclone-like request. This does not assert that every experimental finding was expected or resolve the initial objective of cyclopyrrolone screening.

limits: Cyclopyrrolone/zopiclone program motivation rests on Wermuth's retrospective; his 2006 and 2008 descriptions frame screening differently. The earlier patent discloses chemistry and series-level pharmacology but not the origin narrative. Do not claim that a receptor-binding assay was used at the start of the early-1970s program.

Imidazopyridine/zolpidem's 1978 inspiration rests on Kaplan's first-person retrospective. The patent corroborates a later series disclosure and named inventors, not the full recalled causal sequence or the distribution of intellectual credit.
The class-level judgment concerns the two assigned founding branches. It does not establish the origin of every other GABA-A hypnotic or of all later compounds.
conflicts: Wermuth's 2006 article explicitly describes a benzodiazepine-profile-directed search for zopiclone, whereas his 2008 chapter places zopiclone under extensive screening generally framed as lacking a prior hypothesis and labels its figure random screening. These are not independent accounts and may describe different stages or use terms inconsistently; the precise initial objective is unresolved, not evidence for design from scratch.

Kaplan disputes how the 2013 New Yorker article and other accounts distribute intellectual credit for zolpidem. The patent names both Kaplan and George; these materials do not independently resolve individual priority.

Wermuth summarizes a zolpidem screening search as early 1980s, whereas Kaplan dates his conceptual project to 1978. These may refer to distinct stages, but their exact reconciliation is unverified. Wermuth also combines early-1970s zopiclone discovery with binding-profile language; the 1972-priority patent describes behavioral tests but does not date a receptor-binding assay.
gaps: The 1978 Jeanmart–Cotrel synthesis report and 1979 Blanchard et al. zopiclone-binding report were located but not read. Later 1983 and 1985 pharmacology papers were read only as abstracts.

No contemporaneous narrative documenting the cyclopyrrolone program's first observation, chemical lead, exact screening objective or sequence, or selection experiment was obtained; the retrospective screening descriptions remain in tension.
Kaplan's described 1978 written project and associated original laboratory notes were not obtained; the patent does not independently establish the recalled conceptual sequence.
A complete resolution of personal credit, the chronology of specific binding assays, and later analogue-specific trajectories is outside this class collection.
